Boundary Mass and the Soft-to-Hard Limit in Mixture-of-Experts

Reza Rastegar ††thanks: Email: reza.j.rastegar@gmail.com, Bellevue, WA, USA Affiliation: Meta Platform, Inc.
Abstract

Softmax-routed mixture-of-experts models approach hard routing as the temperature tends to zero, but this limit is singular near routing ties. This paper studies that singularity at the population level for squared-loss MoE regression. The central object is the boundary mass, namely the probability that the top two router scores are separated by only a small margin. Under smoothness and transversality assumptions on the router and input law, we prove coarea/tube estimates showing that this mass is linear in the slab width, with leading constant given by a surface integral over the routing interface in the binary case. These estimates yield quantitative soft-to-hard risk bounds and, under compactness and uniform margin control, Γ\Gamma-convergence of the soft objectives to the hard-routing objective. The main conclusion is that the zero-temperature limit is controlled by a thin geometric layer around routing interfaces, not by the full input space. We then use this geometric core in two more model-dependent directions. In a teacher–student setting, we prove a conditional landscape-transfer principle showing that, when the profiled hard-routing problem has favorable identifiability and curvature and the relevant derivatives transfer at boundary-layer scale, small-temperature soft routing inherits approximate teacher recovery and strict-saddle behavior away from teacher-equivalent partitions. We also give a reduced two-expert Gaussian calculation that illustrates a local symmetry-breaking mechanism aligned with the teacher separator.

1 Introduction

Mixture–of–experts (MoE) models have a long history as architectures for conditional prediction. The original adaptive and hierarchical mixtures of local experts used learned gating networks to combine specialized predictors in an input-dependent way [6, 7]; see also the survey [11]. In modern deep learning, the same idea has become a central form of conditional computation, where a large pool of parameters is available but only a small subset of experts is substantially activated for a given input. Sparsely gated MoE layers and Switch Transformers showed how this mechanism can increase model capacity while keeping the active computation per example relatively controlled [8, 3]. This practical success has also led to a growing theoretical literature on routing, identifiability, estimation, optimization, and expressivity in MoE and gated models [16, 17, 12, 13, 14, 18, 20, 24].

The present paper focuses on a narrower geometric issue that is already visible in the basic MoE model. Existing theory has clarified how gating affects identifiability and estimation rates in statistical mixture-of-experts models [14, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23]. It has also studied how routing can be learned, stabilized, or related to clustering and specialization in stylized optimization settings [16, 17, 12, 13, 15], and how conditional computation changes the expressive or computational capacity of neural architectures [8, 3, 24]. These results explain why MoE models can be statistically, computationally, or expressively attractive. They do not, however, by themselves isolate the singular perturbation created when a smooth softmax router is driven to a hard router by sending the temperature to zero. In particular, they do not give a population-level calculus for how much of the soft objective can differ from the hard objective because of inputs lying close to routing ties.

This is the point at which the present paper enters. It treats the soft-to-hard transition as a boundary-layer problem. A router decides which expert, or which weighted combination of experts, should be used at a given input. This conditional structure is the source of the model’s expressive power, because different regions of the input space can be represented by different predictors. The same structure is also the source of a basic mathematical difficulty. When the router is a softmax with temperature τ>0\tau>0, decreasing τ\tau makes the model look more and more like a hard-routing model. Away from routing ties this passage is harmless, because the losing experts receive exponentially small weight. Near a tie, however, two or more experts may receive comparable weight even when τ\tau is very small. Thus the zero-temperature limit is not controlled uniformly over the whole input space. It is controlled by a thin layer around the router’s decision interfaces.

We write XX for an input drawn from its population law. The router parameter is denoted by ϕ\phi, the collection of expert parameters by θ\theta, and the temperature by τ>0\tau>0. For input xx, the router assigns expert kk the score, or logit, ak​(x,ϕ)a_{k}(x;\phi). The soft population risk at temperature τ\tau is denoted by Lτ​(θ,ϕ)L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi), and the hard-routing risk obtained by sending τ\tau to zero is denoted by L0​(θ,ϕ)L_{0}(\theta,\phi). The main question is how, and in what sense, LτL_{\tau} approaches L0L_{0} as τ↓0\tau\downarrow 0.

The quantity that answers this question is the top–two margin. For a fixed router parameter ϕ\phi, let Δ⁡(x,ϕ)\Delta(x;\phi) be the difference between the largest and second-largest values among the scores {ak​(x,ϕ)}k=1K\{a_{k}(x;\phi)\}_{k=1}^{K}. For a margin width w>0w>0, the probability

ℙ⁡(Δ⁡(X,ϕ)≤w)\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta(X;\phi)\leq w\bigr)

is the mass of inputs whose routing decision is within score distance ww of a tie. We call this boundary mass. Its importance comes from a simple decomposition. On the set where Δ⁡(X,ϕ)\Delta(X;\phi) is much larger than τ\tau, softmax routing and hard routing differ only by exponentially small tails. On the set where Δ⁡(X,ϕ)=O⁡(τ)\Delta(X;\phi)=O(\tau), the two predictors can differ at first order. The low-temperature problem is therefore reduced to estimating how much population mass lies in these O⁡(τ)O(\tau) routing slabs.

The first contribution is a geometric estimate for this mass. Under smoothness of the router, regularity of the input density, and a nonvanishing transverse gradient at the interfaces, the probability of a thin routing slab is proportional to its width. In the binary case, Proposition 3.5 gives the first-order expansion and identifies the constant as a coarea surface integral over the decision surface. Lemma 3.6 records the corresponding one-interface tube formula. Proposition 3.7 then converts the pairwise tube estimates into a global bound for the top–two margin. Example 3.8 makes the same constant explicit for a linear router under a Gaussian input law. The message of these results is that, for regular routers, the part of the input space that can obstruct the hard-routing approximation has probability of order τ\tau.

The second contribution is to turn this geometric estimate into a variational statement about risks. Corollary 4.4 shows that, for a fixed regular router and bounded responses and experts, the soft and hard population risks differ by O⁡(τ)O(\tau). The uniform version is Theorem 4.5. There the assumption is that the top–two margin satisfies, uniformly over the relevant router class, the tail bound

ℙ⁡(Δ⁡(X,ϕ)≤t)≤C​tα,\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta(X;\phi)\leq t\bigr)\leq Ct^{\alpha},

where C>0C>0 and α>0\alpha>0 are constants. Under boundedness of the response and expert outputs, this gives

supθ,ϕ|Lτ​(θ,ϕ)−L0​(θ,ϕ)|≤Csh​τα\sup_{\theta,\phi}\left\lvert L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\right\rvert\leq C_{\mathrm{sh}}\tau^{\alpha}

for a finite constant CshC_{\mathrm{sh}}. Theorem 4.7 strengthens the conclusion from uniform risk approximation to Γ\Gamma-convergence on compact parameter spaces. Consequently, small-temperature soft objectives select the hard-routing objective as their variational limit, so almost minimizers of LτL_{\tau} have cluster points that minimize L0L_{0}.

The third contribution is conditional and more model dependent. In a teacher–student setting, Theorem 5.17 shows how favorable geometry of a profiled hard-routing problem can be inherited by the small-temperature soft objective. Here “profiled” means that, after a router-induced partition is fixed, the expert parameters are optimized out and the remaining landscape is studied over partitions. The theorem is intentionally stated as a transfer principle, not as a generic benign-landscape theorem for all MoEs. It assumes a realizable teacher, a specialization gap that makes confidently wrong routing costly except on a small exceptional set, favorable hard-routing geometry, and first- and second-order soft-to-hard derivative transfer. Under these inputs, global minimizers of the soft objective recover the teacher partition and experts up to permutation, with errors controlled by boundary mass, the specialization-gap exception, and the softness scale. Non-teacher-equivalent critical points inherit negative curvature from the profiled hard problem.

The final technical component is a reduced Gaussian calculation for symmetry breaking. Proposition 6.3 studies a two-expert model near a balanced router and linearizes the router update when the experts already have a small contrast. In that reduced setting, the symmetric router is linearly unstable in a direction correlated with the teacher separator. This calculation is not used to prove the landscape-transfer theorem. Its narrower purpose is to give a concrete local mechanism by which specialization can begin, in a way that is consistent with the boundary-interface interpretation developed earlier.

The resulting contribution is therefore complementary rather than competing with those lines of work. The paper does not prove new finite-sample rates for a fixed statistical MoE family, does not analyze a particular training algorithm for sparse conditional computation, and does not establish a new expressivity theorem. Instead, it supplies a geometric module that can be placed between softmax-gated MoE theory and hard-routing or partition-based intuition. If a prior analysis identifies a meaningful router, a recoverable teacher partition, or a favorable hard-routing landscape, the results here quantify the additional error introduced by replacing hard routing with temperature-τ\tau soft routing. Conversely, they show that the obstruction to such a replacement is not the ambient dimension or the full input distribution by itself, but the probability mass of the O⁡(τ)O(\tau) slabs around routing interfaces.

The assumptions are organized according to this separation. The coarea and tube estimates require only interface regularity and density control. The quantitative soft-to-hard and Γ\Gamma-convergence results require uniform margin tails, boundedness, compactness, and continuity. The teacher–student theorem adds the extra assumptions needed to transfer a favorable profiled hard landscape to the soft objective. This tiered structure is deliberate. It separates the unconditional boundary-layer calculus from the conditional conclusions about recovery and strict saddles.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the population MoE model, notation, and standing assumptions. Section 3 proves the boundary-mass and coarea estimates and includes the Gaussian linear-router calculation. Section 4 proves the quantitative soft-to-hard risk comparison and the Γ\Gamma-convergence theorem. Section 5 develops the conditional landscape-transfer principle. Section 6 presents the reduced Gaussian symmetry-breaking calculation. Section 7 discusses scope, interpretation, and open directions.

2 Population MoE model and notation

This section introduces the population-level Mixture-of-Experts model studied in the remainder of the paper and fixes the notation used thereafter. The main results concern scalar squared-loss regression under a smooth input law. We therefore state the setup directly at that level. Empirical risk, regularization, and finite-sample fluctuations are important for training practice, but they are not analyzed in this paper.

Let 𝒳⊆ℝd\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be the input space, equipped with the Euclidean norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|, and let (X,Y)(X,Y) have joint law 𝖯\mathsf{P} on 𝒳×ℝ\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R}. Its XX-marginal is denoted by PXP_{X}. For events A⊆𝒳A\subseteq\mathcal{X} depending only on XX, we write interchangeably PX​(A)P_{X}(A) and ℙ⁡(A)\mathbb{P}(A). For a scalar predictor f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}, the population squared-loss risk is

ℛ⁡(f):=𝔼(X,Y)∼𝖯​[(Y−f⁡(X))2].\mathcal{R}(f):=\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim\mathsf{P}}\bigl[(Y-f(X))^{2}\bigr]. (2.1)

Unless explicitly stated otherwise, expectations are taken with respect to the joint law 𝖯\mathsf{P}, while probabilities involving only XX are written either as PX​(⋅)P_{X}(\cdot) or, equivalently, as ℙ⁡(⋅)\mathbb{P}(\cdot).

We now introduce the MoE architecture itself. Fix an integer K≥2K\geq 2 as the number of experts, and write expert indices as k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}. We let Θk\Theta_{k} denote the parameter space of expert kk and Φ\Phi the parameter space of the router. An MoE predictor is determined by a family of scalar expert maps fk​(⋅,θk):𝒳→ℝf_{k}(\cdot;\theta_{k}):\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} with θk∈Θk\theta_{k}\in\Theta_{k}, together with a router parameter ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi that assigns input-dependent weights to those experts through a logit map

a⁡(x,ϕ)=(a1​(x,ϕ),…,aK​(x,ϕ))∈ℝK.a(x;\phi)=\bigl(a_{1}(x;\phi),\dots,a_{K}(x;\phi)\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{K}.

For τ>0\tau>0, the router produces the temperature-τ\tau softmax weights

pk(τ)(x;ϕ):=exp⁡(ak​(x,ϕ)/τ)∑j=1Kexp⁡(aj​(x,ϕ)/τ),k=1,…,K.p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\ :=\ \frac{\exp\!\bigl(a_{k}(x;\phi)/\tau\bigr)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp\!\bigl(a_{j}(x;\phi)/\tau\bigr)},\qquad k=1,\dots,K. (2.2)

These weights define the soft MoE predictor

fτ​(x,θ,ϕ):=∑k=1Kpk(τ)​(x,ϕ)​fk​(x,θk).f_{\tau}(x;\theta,\phi)\ :=\ \sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\,f_{k}(x;\theta_{k}). (2.3)

As τ↓0\tau\downarrow 0, the weight vector p(τ)​(x,ϕ)p^{(\tau)}(x;\phi) concentrates on the maximizing logits, so the soft model approaches a hard-routing rule whenever the argmax is unique. The object of study is the population risk ℛ⁡(fτ​(⋅,θ,ϕ))\mathcal{R}(f_{\tau}(\cdot;\theta,\phi)). Equivalently, in the notation used below, we write this risk as Lτ​(θ,ϕ)L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi). The analysis does not make claims about empirical minimization, finite-sample generalization, or the effect of auxiliary regularizers such as load-balancing and entropy penalties. This restriction keeps the focus on the population geometry of the routing interface.

The basic geometric quantities already appear at this level. For a fixed router parameter ϕ\phi, let

a(1)​(x,ϕ)≥a(2)​(x,ϕ)≥⋯≥a(K)​(x,ϕ)a_{(1)}(x;\phi)\geq a_{(2)}(x;\phi)\geq\cdots\geq a_{(K)}(x;\phi)

denote the ordered logits. The top–two margin is

Δ⁡(x,ϕ):=a(1)​(x,ϕ)−a(2)​(x,ϕ)≥ 0.\Delta(x;\phi)\ :=\ a_{(1)}(x;\phi)-a_{(2)}(x;\phi)\ \geq\ 0. (2.4)

Large values of Δ⁡(x,ϕ)\Delta(x;\phi) indicate that the winning expert is well separated from the runner-up, hence that routing is locally stable. The corresponding hard routing rule is the set-valued map

ℳ⁡(x,ϕ):=arg⁡maxk∈{1,…,K}​ak​(x,ϕ),\mathcal{M}(x;\phi)\ :=\ \arg\max_{k\in\{1,\dots,K\}}a_{k}(x;\phi),

and the routing boundary, or tie set, is

𝒯⁡(ϕ):={x∈𝒳:|ℳ⁡(x,ϕ)|≥2}={x∈𝒳:Δ⁡(x,ϕ)=0}.\mathcal{T}(\phi)\ :=\ \{x\in\mathcal{X}:\ |\mathcal{M}(x;\phi)|\geq 2\}\ =\ \{x\in\mathcal{X}:\ \Delta(x;\phi)=0\}. (2.5)

Away from 𝒯⁡(ϕ)\mathcal{T}(\phi) the winning expert is unique, and hard routing is locally constant in xx under mild regularity of the logits.

For later coarea estimates it is useful to track not only the top–two gap but also the smallest pairwise logit separation,

Δmin​(x,ϕ):=mink≠ℓ⁡|ak​(x,ϕ)−aℓ​(x,ϕ)|.\Delta_{\min}(x;\phi):=\min_{k\neq\ell}\left\lvert a_{k}(x;\phi)-a_{\ell}(x;\phi)\right\rvert.

Given a width parameter w>0w>0, we therefore introduce the two boundary-mass profiles

BMϕtop​(w):=ℙ⁡(Δ⁡(X,ϕ)≤w),BMϕpair​(w):=ℙ⁡(Δmin​(X,ϕ)≤w).\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{top}}_{\phi}(w):=\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta(X;\phi)\leq w\bigr),\qquad\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\phi}(w):=\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta_{\min}(X;\phi)\leq w\bigr).

These are two views of the same underlying phenomenon, namely the amount of probability lying in a thin neighborhood of the routing interfaces. The top–two margin is the natural object for soft-versus-hard routing, because it measures how close the winner is to the runner-up. The pairwise quantity is technically convenient when the geometry is decomposed into unions of pairwise slabs. When a tolerance ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2) and temperature τ\tau are fixed, we write

κε:=log⁡(1−εε),\kappa_{\varepsilon}:=\log\!\Bigl(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Bigr),

so that the ambiguity region at temperature τ\tau corresponds to a width of order w=κε​τw=\kappa_{\varepsilon}\tau.

This viewpoint explains why the margin distribution controls the soft-to-hard limit. Fix (x,ϕ)(x,\phi) and assume the maximizing logit is unique, so that Δ⁡(x,ϕ)>0\Delta(x;\phi)>0. A direct softmax estimate gives

∑j≠k⋆​(x,ϕ)pj(τ)(x;ϕ)≤(K−1)exp(−Δ(x;ϕ)/τ),\sum_{j\neq k^{\star}(x;\phi)}p_{j}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\leq(K-1)\exp\bigl(-\Delta(x;\phi)/\tau\bigr),

where k⋆​(x,ϕ)k^{\star}(x;\phi) denotes the unique maximizing expert index. In particular, p(τ)​(x,ϕ)→ek⋆​(x,ϕ)p^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\to e_{k^{\star}(x;\phi)} as τ↓0\tau\downarrow 0. Thus the integrated discrepancy between soft and hard routing is governed by the amount of input mass for which Δ⁡(X,ϕ)\Delta(X;\phi) is small, which is exactly the boundary-mass profile above.

Two structural symmetries will matter later. First, the parameterization is invariant under permutations of the experts. If π\pi is a permutation of {1,…,K}\{1,\dots,K\} and one simultaneously relabels the expert parameters and the router outputs by π\pi, then the resulting predictor fτf_{\tau} is unchanged. Consequently, any isolated minimizer comes with at least K!K! equivalent copies. Second, the logits are defined only up to a common translation. Replacing ak​(x,ϕ)a_{k}(x;\phi) by ak​(x,ϕ)+c​(x)a_{k}(x;\phi)+c(x) for an arbitrary scalar function c⁡(x)c(x) leaves the softmax weights unchanged, so one may fix this gauge when convenient, for example by enforcing ∑k=1Kak​(x,ϕ)=0\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_{k}(x;\phi)=0.

We close the section by recording the standing regularity conditions that will be used later. These assumptions are modest and mainly keep the later geometric arguments from being interrupted by routine measurability or integrability checks.

Assumption 2.1 (Measurability and integrability).

For each temperature τ>0\tau>0 and parameters (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) under consideration, the map x↦fτ​(x,θ,ϕ)x\mapsto f_{\tau}(x;\theta,\phi) is measurable and 𝔼⁡[(Y−fτ​(X,θ,ϕ))2]<∞\mathbb{E}[(Y-f_{\tau}(X;\theta,\phi))^{2}]<\infty.

Assumption 2.1 is largely bookkeeping. It ensures that the population risk is well defined for the parameter values under discussion.

Assumption 2.2 (Local regularity of logits).

When we discuss geometric properties of 𝒯⁡(ϕ)\mathcal{T}(\phi) (e.g. codimension, tubular neighborhoods), we assume a⁡(⋅,ϕ)a(\cdot;\phi) is locally Lipschitz (or C1C^{1}) on 𝒳⊆ℝd\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Assumption 2.2 enters only when we study the geometry of routing boundaries. The later probabilistic soft-to-hard bounds are driven by the margin distribution and do not require this smoothness by themselves.

3 Boundary-layer geometry and coarea control

We start with the geometric estimate that drives the rest of the paper. The basic issue is simple. One wants to know how much probability sits near the router’s moving decision interfaces. That narrow layer is where soft routing departs from hard routing, and it is also the only place where a small change in the partition can have first-order effect on the risk. For that reason this section stands on its own, before any teacher–student specialization. It develops the coarea control of boundary layers, extracts the first small-width asymptotics, and records the margin-tail estimate that later lets us treat soft-routing effects as small.

3.1 Boundary mass and coarea formula

We work on an input domain 𝒳⊆ℝd\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}. (This is the same space denoted by 𝒳\mathcal{X} in Section 2; from here on we use the shorter notation 𝒳\mathcal{X}.) We continue to write PXP_{X} for the marginal law of XX and pXp_{X} for its density when that density exists. We consider router scores (logits) ak​(⋅,ϕ):𝒳→ℝa_{k}(\cdot;\phi):\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}, k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K, and temperature τ>0\tau>0. Throughout this subsection the router parameter ϕ\phi is fixed.

For each pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell) with k≠ℓk\neq\ell, define the pairwise score difference

Sk​ℓ​(x,ϕ):=ak​(x,ϕ)−aℓ​(x,ϕ),x∈𝒳.S_{k\ell}(x;\phi):=a_{k}(x;\phi)-a_{\ell}(x;\phi),\qquad x\in\mathcal{X}. (3.1)

When no ambiguity can arise, we abbreviate Sk​ℓ​(x,ϕ)S_{k\ell}(x;\phi) by Sk​ℓ​(x)S_{k\ell}(x). The decision surface between experts kk and ℓ\ell is

𝒮k​ℓ​(ϕ):={x∈𝒳:Sk​ℓ​(x,ϕ)=0}.\mathcal{S}_{k\ell}(\phi):=\{x\in\mathcal{X}:S_{k\ell}(x;\phi)=0\}. (3.2)

For the fixed router parameter used in this subsection, we also write 𝒮k​ℓ\mathcal{S}_{k\ell} for 𝒮k​ℓ​(ϕ)\mathcal{S}_{k\ell}(\phi). The stronger tubular regularity needed for the coarea expansion is stated explicitly in Assumption 3.4; the present notation only identifies the pairwise interfaces to which that assumption will be applied.

Let pXp_{X} denote the density of PXP_{X} with respect to Lebesgue measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. It will also be convenient to introduce a global margin function, which measures, in terms of pairwise logit differences, how close xx is to at least one decision surface.

Δmin​(x,ϕ):=mink≠ℓ⁡|Sk​ℓ​(x)|,x∈𝒳.\Delta_{\min}(x;\phi):=\min_{k\neq\ell}|S_{k\ell}(x)|,\qquad x\in\mathcal{X}. (3.3)

Small values of Δmin​(X,ϕ)\Delta_{\min}(X;\phi) correspond to inputs lying in thin slabs around at least one decision surface.

Definition 3.1 (Pairwise boundary mass profile).

For w>0w>0 recall the pairwise boundary mass profile

BMϕpair​(w):=ℙ⁡(Δmin​(X,ϕ)≤w),\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\phi}(w):=\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta_{\min}(X;\phi)\leq w\bigr), (3.4)

Fix ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2) and set κε:=log⁡(1−εε)\kappa_{\varepsilon}:=\log\!\Bigl(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Bigr). Define the pairwise ambiguity events

Ak​ℓ(ε,τ):={exp⁡(ak​(X,ϕ)/τ)exp⁡(ak​(X,ϕ)/τ)+exp⁡(aℓ​(X,ϕ)/τ)∈[ε,1−ε]},k≠ℓ.A_{k\ell}(\varepsilon,\tau):=\Bigl\{\frac{\exp(a_{k}(X;\phi)/\tau)}{\exp(a_{k}(X;\phi)/\tau)+\exp(a_{\ell}(X;\phi)/\tau)}\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]\Bigr\},\qquad k\neq\ell. (3.5)

Then Ak​ℓ​(ε,τ)A_{k\ell}(\varepsilon,\tau) is equivalent to |Sk​ℓ​(X)|≤κε​τ\left\lvert S_{k\ell}(X)\right\rvert\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon}\,\tau, and therefore the temperature-parametrized boundary mass is simply

BMεpair​(τ):=ℙ⁡(⋃1≤k<ℓ≤KAk​ℓ​(ε,τ))=BMϕpair​(κε​τ).\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau):=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigcup_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}A_{k\ell}(\varepsilon,\tau)\Bigr)=\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\phi}(\kappa_{\varepsilon}\,\tau). (3.6)

For a different input law RR on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the same definition applies with R⁡(⋅)R(\cdot) in place of PX​(⋅)P_{X}(\cdot).

In words, BMεpair​(τ)\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau) is the probability that for at least one pair of experts the pairwise softmax probability lies in the ambiguous range [ε,1−ε][\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]; equivalently, some score difference is O⁡(τ)O(\tau). For small τ\tau this ambiguity occurs only in thin neighborhoods of decision surfaces.

Remark 3.2 (Equivalent slab form).

For any fixed ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2), recall κε:=log⁡(1−εε)>0\kappa_{\varepsilon}:=\log\!\bigl(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\bigr)>0. Then for each pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell),

Ak​ℓ(ε,τ)⟺|Sk​ℓ(X)|≤κετ,A_{k\ell}(\varepsilon,\tau)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad|S_{k\ell}(X)|\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon}\,\tau,

and therefore

BMεpair​(τ)=ℙ⁡(min1≤k<ℓ≤K⁡|Sk​ℓ​(X)|≤κε​τ)=BMϕpair​(κε​τ).\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\min_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}|S_{k\ell}(X)|\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon}\,\tau\Bigr)=\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\phi}(\kappa_{\varepsilon}\,\tau).

This is the precise sense in which BMεpair​(τ)\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau) measures the probability mass of an O⁡(τ)O(\tau)-thick union of slabs around the decision surfaces {𝒮k​ℓ}\{\mathcal{S}_{k\ell}\}, expressed through the pairwise logit differences.

For the binary case K=2K=2 the definition simplifies considerably and gives a concrete geometric picture.

Remark 3.3 (Binary case).

When K=2K=2, we have

ea1​(x,ϕ)/τea1​(x,ϕ)/τ+ea2​(x,ϕ)/τ=σ⁡(S12​(x)τ),\frac{e^{a_{1}(x;\phi)/\tau}}{e^{a_{1}(x;\phi)/\tau}+e^{a_{2}(x;\phi)/\tau}}=\sigma\Bigl(\frac{S_{12}(x)}{\tau}\Bigr),

where σ⁡(t)=(1+e−t)−1\sigma(t)=(1+e^{-t})^{-1} is the logistic function. Then

BMεpair​(τ)=ℙ⁡(S12​(X)∈[aε​(τ),bε​(τ)]),\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\mathbb{P}\bigl(S_{12}(X)\in[a_{\varepsilon}(\tau),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)]\bigr),

where aε​(τ)=τ​log⁡(ε/(1−ε))a_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\tau\log(\varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)) and bε​(τ)=τ​log⁡((1−ε)/ε)b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\tau\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon). Thus BMεpair​(τ)\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau) is exactly the probability mass in an O⁡(τ)O(\tau)-thick slab around the decision surface 𝒮12\mathcal{S}_{12}.

We now make the regularity assumption needed to apply the coarea formula.

Assumption 3.4 (Regular router, density, and tubular level sets).

For each k≠ℓk\neq\ell, the function Sk​ℓ:𝒳→ℝS_{k\ell}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} is C2C^{2} on a neighborhood of the tube {|Sk​ℓ|≤δreg}\{|S_{k\ell}|\leq\delta_{\mathrm{reg}}\} for some δreg>0\delta_{\mathrm{reg}}>0. There is a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that

‖∇Sk​ℓ​(x)‖≥c0for almost every x∈𝒳 with ​|Sk​ℓ​(x)|≤δreg,\left\lVert\nabla S_{k\ell}(x)\right\rVert\geq c_{0}\qquad\text{for almost every $x\in\mathcal{X}$ with }|S_{k\ell}(x)|\leq\delta_{\mathrm{reg}}, (3.7)

where “almost every” is with respect to Lebesgue measure. The density pXp_{X} is continuous and bounded on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. In addition, the nearby level sets Sk​ℓ−1​(t)S_{k\ell}^{-1}(t), |t|≤δreg|t|\leq\delta_{\mathrm{reg}}, admit a regular tubular parametrization by normal flow away from a set of ℋd−1\mathcal{H}^{d-1}-measure zero, and the corresponding surface Jacobians are locally dominated by an integrable function. For the estimates below, the needed consequence is that the level-set profile

Fk​ℓ​(t):=∫Sk​ℓ−1​(t)pX​(x)‖∇Sk​ℓ​(x)‖​d​ℋd−1​(x)F_{k\ell}(t):=\int_{S_{k\ell}^{-1}(t)}\frac{p_{X}(x)}{\left\lVert\nabla S_{k\ell}(x)\right\rVert}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x) (3.8)

is finite for |t|≤δreg|t|\leq\delta_{\mathrm{reg}} and continuous at t=0t=0.

Assumption 3.4 combines two familiar requirements. First, tie surfaces should not become flat in a way that kills the transverse gradient. Second, the input law should not pile up on lower-dimensional sets near those surfaces. Together these conditions keep the interfaces nondegenerate in the only region that matters for the tube estimate. For smooth routers the lower bound (3.7) is the expected situation away from a negligible set of critical points, and the density condition covers continuous data laws as well as discrete data after a small amount of smoothing. Once these ingredients are in place, the usual tubular-neighborhood and coarea arguments give linear control of boundary-tube mass.

One concrete way to diagnose failure of this assumption is to examine the empirical margin histogram together with the distribution of ‖∇xSk​ℓ​(X,ϕ)‖\|\nabla_{x}S_{k\ell}(X;\phi)\| on samples for which |Sk​ℓ​(X,ϕ)||S_{k\ell}(X;\phi)| is small. Persistent mass near zero combined with tiny gradients is the signature of a nearly degenerate interface.

The point of Assumption 3.4 is that it extends the nonvanishing-gradient condition from the interface itself to an entire tubular neighborhood {|Sk​ℓ|≤δreg}\{|S_{k\ell}|\leq\delta_{\mathrm{reg}}\}. That is the scale on which the argument actually runs, because one needs uniform control of pX/‖∇Sk​ℓ‖p_{X}/\|\nabla S_{k\ell}\| on nearby level sets rather than only on the zero set. The continuity of the profile in (3.8) is automatic in many standard compact C2C^{2} situations, and it is the precise regularity needed for the first-order tube expansion below.

Under Assumption 3.4, each level set Sk​ℓ−1​(t)S_{k\ell}^{-1}(t) is a smooth hypersurface for |t|≤δreg|t|\leq\delta_{\mathrm{reg}} (up to a null set), and the coarea formula allows us to integrate over slabs by first integrating along level sets and then over the level value tt.

The next result quantifies the mass of O⁡(τ)O(\tau)-thick slabs in the binary case and identifies an explicit geometric constant.

Proposition 3.5 (Coarea expansion for binary routing boundary mass).

Suppose Assumption 3.4 holds and K=2K=2. Then for each ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2) we have

BMεpair​(τ)=Cε​τ+o⁡(τ),τ↓0,\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=C_{\varepsilon}\,\tau+o(\tau),\qquad\tau\downarrow 0,

where

Cε=2​log⁡(1−εε)​∫𝒮12pX​(x)‖∇S12​(x)‖​d​ℋd−1​(x),C_{\varepsilon}=2\log\!\Bigl(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)\int_{\mathcal{S}_{12}}\frac{p_{X}(x)}{\left\lVert\nabla S_{12}(x)\right\rVert}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x),

and ℋd−1\mathcal{H}^{d-1} denotes (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional Hausdorff (surface) measure.

Proof.

Let aε​(τ)=τ​log⁡(ε/(1−ε))a_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\tau\log(\varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)) and bε​(τ)=τ​log⁡((1−ε)/ε)b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\tau\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon). Then by the binary representation in the remark above,

BMεpair​(τ)=ℙ⁡(S12​(X)∈[aε​(τ),bε​(τ)])=∫𝒳𝟙[aε​(τ),bε​(τ)]​(S12​(x))​pX​(x)​𝑑x.\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\mathbb{P}\bigl(S_{12}(X)\in[a_{\varepsilon}(\tau),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)]\bigr)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\mathds{1}_{[a_{\varepsilon}(\tau),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)]}(S_{12}(x))p_{X}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.

We now introduce the function

hτ​(x):=𝟙[aε​(τ),bε​(τ)]​(S12​(x))​pX​(x)‖∇S12​(x)‖,h_{\tau}(x):=\mathds{1}_{[a_{\varepsilon}(\tau),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)]}(S_{12}(x))\frac{p_{X}(x)}{\left\lVert\nabla S_{12}(x)\right\rVert},

which is measurable and bounded for small τ\tau because pXp_{X} is bounded and ‖∇S12‖\left\lVert\nabla S_{12}\right\rVert is bounded away from zero on the relevant level sets by (3.7). Then

BMεpair​(τ)=∫𝒳hτ​(x)​‖∇S12​(x)‖​𝑑x.\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}h_{\tau}(x)\,\left\lVert\nabla S_{12}(x)\right\rVert\,\mathrm{d}x.

By the coarea formula for C1C^{1} (indeed Lipschitz) functions [2, Theorem 3.4.2],

∫𝒳hτ​(x)​‖∇S12​(x)‖​𝑑x=∫ℝ[∫S12−1​(t)hτ​(x)​d​ℋd−1​(x)]​𝑑t.\int_{\mathcal{X}}h_{\tau}(x)\,\left\lVert\nabla S_{12}(x)\right\rVert\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\biggl[\int_{S_{12}^{-1}(t)}h_{\tau}(x)\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x)\biggr]\mathrm{d}t.

By the definition of hτh_{\tau}, the integrand vanishes unless t∈[aε​(τ),bε​(τ)]t\in[a_{\varepsilon}(\tau),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)]. Hence

BMεpair​(τ)=∫aε​(τ)bε​(τ)[∫S12−1​(t)pX​(x)‖∇S12​(x)‖​d​ℋd−1​(x)]​𝑑t.\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\int_{a_{\varepsilon}(\tau)}^{b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)}\biggl[\int_{S_{12}^{-1}(t)}\frac{p_{X}(x)}{\left\lVert\nabla S_{12}(x)\right\rVert}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x)\biggr]\mathrm{d}t.

Let F​(t):=F12​(t)F(t):=F_{12}(t) be the level-set profile from (3.8). By Assumption 3.4, F⁡(t)F(t) is finite for |t|≤δreg|t|\leq\delta_{\mathrm{reg}} and continuous at t=0t=0. Fix δ>0\delta>0 small enough that [aε​(τ),bε​(τ)]⊂[−δ,δ]⊂(−δreg,δreg)[a_{\varepsilon}(\tau),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)]\subset[-\delta,\delta]\subset(-\delta_{\mathrm{reg}},\delta_{\mathrm{reg}}) for all sufficiently small τ\tau. For such τ\tau the mean value theorem for integrals applies.

∫aε​(τ)bε​(τ)F⁡(t)​𝑑t=(bε​(τ)−aε​(τ))​F​(ξτ),\int_{a_{\varepsilon}(\tau)}^{b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)}F(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=\bigl(b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)-a_{\varepsilon}(\tau)\bigr)\,F(\xi_{\tau}),

for some ξτ∈[aε​(τ),bε​(τ)]\xi_{\tau}\in[a_{\varepsilon}(\tau),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)]. Because aε​(τ),bε​(τ)→0a_{\varepsilon}(\tau),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)\to 0 as τ↓0\tau\downarrow 0, we have ξτ→0\xi_{\tau}\to 0 and hence F⁡(ξτ)→F⁡(0)F(\xi_{\tau})\to F(0) by continuity of FF. Therefore

BMεpair​(τ)=(bε​(τ)−aε​(τ))​F​(0)+o⁡(bε​(τ)−aε​(τ)).\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\bigl(b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)-a_{\varepsilon}(\tau)\bigr)\,F(0)+o\bigl(b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)-a_{\varepsilon}(\tau)\bigr).

Finally,

bε​(τ)−aε​(τ)=2​τ​log⁡(1−εε),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)-a_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=2\tau\log\Bigl(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Bigr),

which yields the desired linear expansion with

Cε=2​log⁡(1−εε)​F​(0)=2​log⁡(1−εε)​∫𝒮12pX​(x)‖∇S12​(x)‖​d​ℋd−1​(x).C_{\varepsilon}=2\log\Bigl(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)F(0)=2\log\Bigl(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)\int_{\mathcal{S}_{12}}\frac{p_{X}(x)}{\left\lVert\nabla S_{12}(x)\right\rVert}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x).

∎

The proof shows that the constant CεC_{\varepsilon} is simply the geometric surface integral of pX/‖∇S12‖p_{X}/\|\nabla S_{12}\| multiplied by the effective slab width 2​log⁡((1−ε)/ε)2\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon) in score space. More generally, the same argument yields a linear expansion for slabs of arbitrary small thickness.

Lemma 3.6 (General tube formula for a single decision surface).

Suppose Assumption 3.4 holds for a given pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell). Then there exists w0>0w_{0}>0 such that for all w∈(0,w0]w\in(0,w_{0}],

ℙ⁡(|Sk​ℓ​(X)|≤w)=2​w​∫𝒮k​ℓpX​(x)‖∇Sk​ℓ​(x)‖​d​ℋd−1​(x)+o⁡(w),w↓0.\mathbb{P}\bigl(|S_{k\ell}(X)|\leq w\bigr)=2w\int_{\mathcal{S}_{k\ell}}\frac{p_{X}(x)}{\left\lVert\nabla S_{k\ell}(x)\right\rVert}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x)+o(w),\qquad w\downarrow 0.
Proof.

Apply the argument of Proposition 3.5 with [aε​(τ),bε​(τ)][a_{\varepsilon}(\tau),b_{\varepsilon}(\tau)] replaced by [−δ,δ][-\delta,\delta] and S12S_{12} replaced by Sk​ℓS_{k\ell}. This gives

ℙ⁡(|Sk​ℓ​(X)|≤δ)=∫−δδFk​ℓ​(t)​𝑑t,\mathbb{P}\bigl(|S_{k\ell}(X)|\leq\delta\bigr)=\int_{-\delta}^{\delta}F_{k\ell}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t,

where Fk​ℓF_{k\ell} is the profile defined in (3.8). Assumption 3.4 ensures Fk​ℓF_{k\ell} is finite and continuous near 00, so the mean value theorem for integrals gives

∫−δδFk​ℓ​(t)​𝑑t=2​δ​Fk​ℓ​(ξδ)\int_{-\delta}^{\delta}F_{k\ell}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=2\delta\,F_{k\ell}(\xi_{\delta})

for some ξδ∈[−δ,δ]\xi_{\delta}\in[-\delta,\delta]; as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0, ξδ→0\xi_{\delta}\to 0 and Fk​ℓ​(ξδ)→Fk​ℓ​(0)F_{k\ell}(\xi_{\delta})\to F_{k\ell}(0), which yields the desired expansion. ∎

Lemma 3.6 is purely geometric. It says that the probability of falling in a slab of width δ\delta around a smooth hypersurface is proportional, to first order, to δ\delta times a surface integral determined by pXp_{X} and the local slope of the defining function.

For K>2K>2 we can obtain a linear upper bound on the boundary mass by summing the pairwise contributions. Using the events Ak​ℓ​(ε,τ)A_{k\ell}(\varepsilon,\tau) from Definition 3.1, we have

BMεpair​(τ)=ℙ⁡(⋃1≤k<ℓ≤KAk​ℓ​(ε,τ))≤∑1≤k<ℓ≤Kℙ⁡(Ak​ℓ​(ε,τ)).\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigcup_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}A_{k\ell}(\varepsilon,\tau)\Bigr)\leq\sum_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}\mathbb{P}\bigl(A_{k\ell}(\varepsilon,\tau)\bigr).

Each probability ℙ​(Ak​ℓ​(ε,τ))\mathbb{P}(A_{k\ell}(\varepsilon,\tau)) has exactly the same representation as in the binary case with S12S_{12} replaced by Sk​ℓS_{k\ell} and hence satisfies a linear expansion

ℙ⁡(Ak​ℓ​(ε,τ))=Cε,k​ℓ​τ+o⁡(τ),\mathbb{P}\bigl(A_{k\ell}(\varepsilon,\tau)\bigr)=C_{\varepsilon,k\ell}\tau+o(\tau),

with

Cε,k​ℓ=2​log⁡(1−εε)​∫𝒮k​ℓpX​(x)‖∇Sk​ℓ​(x)‖​d​ℋd−1​(x),C_{\varepsilon,k\ell}=2\log\!\Bigl(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)\int_{\mathcal{S}_{k\ell}}\frac{p_{X}(x)}{\left\lVert\nabla S_{k\ell}(x)\right\rVert}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x),

by the same coarea-formula argument. Summing over all pairs we obtain

BMεpair​(τ)≤C~ε​τ+o⁡(τ),C~ε:=∑1≤k<ℓ≤KCε,k​ℓ.\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)\leq\widetilde{C}_{\varepsilon}\tau+o(\tau),\qquad\widetilde{C}_{\varepsilon}:=\sum_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}C_{\varepsilon,k\ell}. (3.9)

Thus, for general KK, the leading constant is controlled by the total surface area of all pairwise decision boundaries weighted by pX/‖∇Sk​ℓ‖p_{X}/\|\nabla S_{k\ell}\|.

The next result extracts a global margin tail bound from this picture. It will be used repeatedly later to control the mass near router boundaries in terms of a single small parameter.

Proposition 3.7 (Global margin tail bound).

Suppose Assumption 3.4 holds. Then there exist constants δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 and Cmargin>0C_{\mathrm{margin}}>0 such that

ℙ⁡(Δmin​(X,ϕ)≤δ)≤Cmargin​δ,0<δ≤δ0,\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta_{\min}(X;\phi)\leq\delta\bigr)\leq C_{\mathrm{margin}}\;\delta,\qquad 0<\delta\leq\delta_{0},

where Δmin\Delta_{\min} is defined in (3.3).

Proof.

By definition of Δmin\Delta_{\min} and a union bound,

ℙ⁡(Δmin​(X,ϕ)≤w)≤∑1≤k<ℓ≤Kℙ⁡(|Sk​ℓ​(X)|≤w).\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta_{\min}(X;\phi)\leq w\bigr)\leq\sum_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}\mathbb{P}\bigl(|S_{k\ell}(X)|\leq w\bigr).

Fix a pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell). By the coarea formula as in Lemma 3.6, for ww sufficiently small we have

ℙ⁡(|Sk​ℓ​(X)|≤w)=∫−wwFk​ℓ​(t)​𝑑t,\mathbb{P}\bigl(|S_{k\ell}(X)|\leq w\bigr)=\int_{-w}^{w}F_{k\ell}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t,

where Fk​ℓ​(t)F_{k\ell}(t) is finite and continuous on a neighborhood of 00 by Assumption 3.4. Hence there exists w0>0w_{0}>0 such that sup|t|≤w0Fk​ℓ​(t)<∞\sup_{|t|\leq w_{0}}F_{k\ell}(t)<\infty, and for all w∈(0,w0]w\in(0,w_{0}],

ℙ⁡(|Sk​ℓ​(X)|≤w)≤2​w​sup|t|≤w0Fk​ℓ​(t)=:Ck​ℓ​w.\mathbb{P}\bigl(|S_{k\ell}(X)|\leq w\bigr)\leq 2w\sup_{|t|\leq w_{0}}F_{k\ell}(t)=:C_{k\ell}\,w.

Summing over all (K2)\binom{K}{2} pairs gives

ℙ⁡(Δmin​(X,ϕ)≤w)≤(∑1≤k<ℓ≤KCk​ℓ)​w,\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta_{\min}(X;\phi)\leq w\bigr)\leq\Bigl(\sum_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}C_{k\ell}\Bigr)w,

so we can take Cmargin:=∑1≤k<ℓ≤KCk​ℓC_{\mathrm{margin}}:=\sum_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}C_{k\ell}. ∎

Proposition 3.7 says that, under mild regularity, the global margin distribution puts at most linear mass near zero. So inputs that sit close to a routing boundary become rare at rate O⁡(δ)O(\delta) as the threshold δ\delta shrinks. Later we will use exactly this fact to treat the O⁡(τ)O(\tau) boundary layer as a perturbative part of the risk.

The following elementary example makes the constant in the coarea expansion explicit. It is also a useful local model for a smooth router, because near a regular interface the score difference is well approximated by its first-order linearization.

Example 3.8 (Binary linear router under a Gaussian input).

Let K=2K=2, let 𝒳=ℝd\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{d}, and suppose X∼N⁡(0,Σ)X\sim N(0,\Sigma) with Σ\Sigma positive definite. Consider a linear score difference

S12​(x,ϕ)=⟨v,x⟩+b,v∈ℝd∖{0},b∈ℝ.S_{12}(x;\phi)=\langle v,x\rangle+b,\qquad v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\},\quad b\in\mathbb{R}. (3.10)

Set σv2:=v⊤​Σ​v\sigma_{v}^{2}:=v^{\top}\Sigma v and write Z:=S12​(X,ϕ)Z:=S_{12}(X;\phi). Then Z∼N⁡(b,σv2)Z\sim N(b,\sigma_{v}^{2}). If Φ\Phi and φN\varphi_{\mathrm{N}} denote the standard normal distribution function and density, respectively, then for every r>0r>0,

ℙ⁡(|S12​(X,ϕ)|≤r)=Φ⁡(r−bσv)−Φ⁡(−r−bσv).\mathbb{P}(|S_{12}(X;\phi)|\leq r)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{r-b}{\sigma_{v}}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{-r-b}{\sigma_{v}}\right). (3.11)

Consequently, as r↓0r\downarrow 0,

ℙ⁡(|S12​(X,ϕ)|≤r)=2​r​φN​(b/σv)σv+o⁡(r).\mathbb{P}(|S_{12}(X;\phi)|\leq r)=2r\,\frac{\varphi_{\mathrm{N}}(b/\sigma_{v})}{\sigma_{v}}+o(r). (3.12)

Taking r=κε​τr=\kappa_{\varepsilon}\tau gives the binary boundary-mass asymptotic

BMεpair​(τ)=2​κε​φN​(b/σv)σv​τ+o⁡(τ),τ↓0.\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\varepsilon}(\tau)=2\kappa_{\varepsilon}\,\frac{\varphi_{\mathrm{N}}(b/\sigma_{v})}{\sigma_{v}}\,\tau+o(\tau),\qquad\tau\downarrow 0. (3.13)

This agrees exactly with Proposition 3.5. Indeed, the decision surface is the hyperplane {x:⟨v,x⟩+b=0}\{x:\langle v,x\rangle+b=0\}, ∇S12=v\nabla S_{12}=v, and the coarea identity gives

∫{S12=0}pX​(x)‖v‖dℋd−1(x)=φN​(b/σv)σv.\int_{\{S_{12}=0\}}\frac{p_{X}(x)}{\|v\|}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x)=\frac{\varphi_{\mathrm{N}}(b/\sigma_{v})}{\sigma_{v}}. (3.14)

Thus the abstract surface integral is simply the density at zero of the projected score S12​(X,ϕ)S_{12}(X;\phi). The example also shows how the coefficient changes with the position and scale of the router, since moving the hyperplane into a low-density region or scaling the logit difference upward reduces the amount of mass in an O⁡(τ)O(\tau) score slab.

For the main results below, the linear upper bound from Proposition 3.7 is the key input. Under additional transversality assumptions one can sharpen this to a full first-order asymptotic for the multi-class boundary mass, but that refinement is not needed for the present theorem chain and is omitted here.

4 The variational zero-temperature limit and Γ\Gamma-convergence

We return in this section to the zero-temperature limit. The earlier comparison estimates already show that, for fixed parameters, the soft risk is close to the hard risk when τ\tau is small. The point of Γ\Gamma-convergence is different, because it upgrades pointwise convergence of functionals to a variational statement about minimizers and almost minimizers. In other words, it identifies the hard-routing problem as the correct limiting optimization problem for the soft family. The compactness assumptions introduced below are precisely what is needed to pass from quantitative soft–hard control to that variational conclusion.

We begin this section by recalling the temperature-τ\tau softmax router associated to scores a⁡(⋅,ϕ)=(a1​(⋅,ϕ),…,aK​(⋅,ϕ))a(\cdot;\phi)=(a_{1}(\cdot;\phi),\dots,a_{K}(\cdot;\phi)).

pk(τ)​(x,ϕ):=exp⁡(ak​(x,ϕ)/τ)∑j=1Kexp⁡(aj​(x,ϕ)/τ),τ>0.p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi):=\frac{\exp(a_{k}(x;\phi)/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(a_{j}(x;\phi)/\tau)},\qquad\tau>0.

The corresponding soft MoE predictor is

hθ,ϕ,τ​(x):=∑k=1Kpk(τ)​(x,ϕ)​fk​(x,θk),h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(x):=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\,f_{k}(x;\theta_{k}),

and the associated population squared-loss risk functional is

Lτ​(θ,ϕ):=𝔼⁡[(Y−hθ,ϕ,τ​(X))2].L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(Y-h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X))^{2}\bigr]. (4.1)

4.1 Hard routing and limiting risk

Given router scores a⁡(⋅,ϕ)a(\cdot;\phi), define the hard router

pk(0)​(x,ϕ):=𝟙k=k⋆​(x,ϕ),k⋆​(x,ϕ):=arg⁡max1≤j≤K​aj​(x,ϕ).p_{k}^{(0)}(x;\phi):=\mathds{1}_{k=k^{\star}(x;\phi)},\qquad k^{\star}(x;\phi):=\arg\max_{1\leq j\leq K}a_{j}(x;\phi).

(For measurability, one can take the canonical tie-break k⋆​(x,ϕ):=min⁡arg⁡maxj​aj​(x,ϕ)k^{\star}(x;\phi):=\min\arg\max_{j}a_{j}(x;\phi). Under the tail/margin condition below we will in fact have PX​(tie)=0P_{X}(\text{tie})=0, so any tie-breaking rule on that null set yields the same risk L0L_{0}.) The corresponding hard MoE predictor is

hθ,ϕ,0​(x):=∑k=1Kpk(0)​(x,ϕ)​fk​(x,θk)=fk⋆​(x,ϕ)​(x,θk⋆​(x,ϕ)).h_{\theta,\phi,0}(x):=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}^{(0)}(x;\phi)\,f_{k}(x;\theta_{k})=f_{k^{\star}(x;\phi)}(x;\theta_{k^{\star}(x;\phi)}).

The limiting risk functional is

L0​(θ,ϕ):=𝔼⁡[(Y−hθ,ϕ,0​(X))2].L_{0}(\theta,\phi):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(Y-h_{\theta,\phi,0}(X))^{2}\bigr]. (4.2)

We aim to show that LτL_{\tau} Γ\Gamma-converges to L0L_{0} as τ→0\tau\to 0 [1], and also to obtain a uniform quantitative bound supθ,ϕ|Lτ​(θ,ϕ)−L0​(θ,ϕ)|≲τα\sup_{\theta,\phi}\left\lvert L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\right\rvert\lesssim\tau^{\alpha} under a margin assumption on router scores.

4.2 Softmax tail bounds

We first record a simple tail bound for the softmax, which quantifies how small non-maximal probabilities become when the score margin is large.

Lemma 4.1 (Softmax tail, pointwise).

Let z=(z1,…,zK)∈ℝKz=(z_{1},\dots,z_{K})\in\mathbb{R}^{K}. Let z(1)≥⋯≥z(K)z_{(1)}\geq\cdots\geq z_{(K)} be the sorted values and let pk​(z,τ)p_{k}(z;\tau) be the softmax weights with temperature τ\tau, i.e. pk​(z,τ)=exp⁡(zk/τ)/∑iexp⁡(zi/τ)p_{k}(z;\tau)=\exp(z_{k}/\tau)/\sum_{i}\exp(z_{i}/\tau). Then for any j≥2j\geq 2,

p(j)(z;τ)≤exp(−(z(1)−z(j))/τ).p_{(j)}(z;\tau)\leq\exp\bigl(-(z_{(1)}-z_{(j)})/\tau\bigr).

In particular,

∑j=2Kp(j)(z;τ)≤(K−1)exp(−Δ(z)/τ),\sum_{j=2}^{K}p_{(j)}(z;\tau)\leq(K-1)\exp\bigl(-\Delta(z)/\tau\bigr),

where Δ⁡(z):=z(1)−z(2)\Delta(z):=z_{(1)}-z_{(2)} is the top-two margin.

Proof.

For each j≥2j\geq 2,

p(j)(z;τ)=exp⁡(z(j)/τ)∑i=1Kexp⁡(z(i)/τ)≤exp⁡(z(j)/τ)exp⁡(z(1)/τ)=exp(−(z(1)−z(j))/τ).p_{(j)}(z;\tau)=\frac{\exp(z_{(j)}/\tau)}{\sum_{i=1}^{K}\exp(z_{(i)}/\tau)}\leq\frac{\exp(z_{(j)}/\tau)}{\exp(z_{(1)}/\tau)}=\exp\bigl(-(z_{(1)}-z_{(j)})/\tau\bigr).

Summing over j≥2j\geq 2 yields the second claim with Δ⁡(z)\Delta(z) defined as above. ∎

4.3 A quantitative soft–hard comparison

Recall the top–two margin of the router logits from Section 2,

Δ⁡(x,ϕ):=a(1)​(x,ϕ)−a(2)​(x,ϕ)≥0,\Delta(x;\phi):=a_{(1)}(x;\phi)-a_{(2)}(x;\phi)\geq 0,

where a(1)​(x,ϕ)≥a(2)​(x,ϕ)≥⋯≥a(K)​(x,ϕ)a_{(1)}(x;\phi)\geq a_{(2)}(x;\phi)\geq\cdots\geq a_{(K)}(x;\phi) are the sorted values of (a1​(x,ϕ),…,aK​(x,ϕ))(a_{1}(x;\phi),\dots,a_{K}(x;\phi)). A positive margin Δ⁡(x,ϕ)>0\Delta(x;\phi)>0 is equivalent to uniqueness of the argmax of a⁡(x,ϕ)a(x;\phi) at xx. The next assumption is the uniform margin condition that drives the soft-to-hard rate. We record it here before using it in the quantitative comparison theorem.

Assumption 4.2 (Uniform moment and margin-tail control).

There exist constants C>0C>0 and α>0\alpha>0 such that, for all admissible (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi),

𝔼⁡[|Y|2+∑k=1K|fk​(X,θk)|2]≤C,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\left\lvert Y\right\rvert^{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\lvert f_{k}(X;\theta_{k})\right\rvert^{2}\bigr]\leq C, (4.3)

and, for all t>0t>0,

ℙ⁡(Δ⁡(X,ϕ)≤t)≤C​tα.\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta(X;\phi)\leq t\bigr)\leq Ct^{\alpha}. (4.4)

Assumption 4.2 gives both uniform integrability and uniform control of the margin distribution near zero. We use it when passing to limits such as τ↓0\tau\downarrow 0 and when making sure the boundary-layer error is not overwhelmed by rare but very large losses. It is automatic for bounded losses, and it also holds for polynomial-growth losses under sub-Gaussian or sub-exponential tails with uniformly controlled model outputs. In heavy-tailed settings one would need a truncated or robust variant of the argument.

To obtain a uniform rate, we impose a global boundedness assumption on the response and expert families. This is not conceptually central; it is simply a convenient way to keep the soft–hard comparison from carrying additional tail terms.

Assumption 4.3 (Uniform boundedness).

There exist finite constants BY,Bf>0B_{Y},B_{f}>0 such that |Y|≤BY\left\lvert Y\right\rvert\leq B_{Y} almost surely and |fk​(x,θk)|≤Bf\left\lvert f_{k}(x;\theta_{k})\right\rvert\leq B_{f} for all kk, all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and all admissible θk\theta_{k}.

Assumption 4.3 is included for convenience. It lets the quantitative soft–hard bounds go through without carrying a separate layer of tail bookkeeping. The condition is natural in classification after label smoothing or clipping, and in regression when labels and predictions are truncated to a fixed range. If the outputs are unbounded, one can usually replace it by moment assumptions plus concentration estimates, but the constants and the proof become noticeably less clean. Before stating the uniform theorem, it is useful to record the direct fixed-router consequence of the coarea control from Section 3. Under Assumption 3.4, the near-tie layer has linear mass, and that already forces an explicit linear soft-to-hard risk bound for bounded outputs.

Corollary 4.4 (Coarea-based O⁡(τ)O(\tau) soft-to-hard bound).

Suppose Assumption 3.4 holds for a fixed router parameter ϕ\phi, the argmax of a⁡(⋅,ϕ)a(\cdot;\phi) is unique PXP_{X}-almost surely, and Assumption 4.3 holds. Then there exist constants τ0>0\tau_{0}>0 and Cco​(ϕ)>0C_{\mathrm{co}}(\phi)>0 such that for every admissible expert parameter θ\theta and every τ∈(0,τ0]\tau\in(0,\tau_{0}],

|Lτ​(θ,ϕ)−L0​(θ,ϕ)|≤Cco​(ϕ)​τ.\left\lvert L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\right\rvert\leq C_{\mathrm{co}}(\phi)\,\tau.
Proof.

Let Δ⁡(x,ϕ)=a(1)​(x,ϕ)−a(2)​(x,ϕ)\Delta(x;\phi)=a_{(1)}(x;\phi)-a_{(2)}(x;\phi) denote the top-two margin. Since Δmin​(x,ϕ)≤Δ⁡(x,ϕ)\Delta_{\min}(x;\phi)\leq\Delta(x;\phi) for every xx, the event {Δ(X;ϕ)≤t}\{\Delta(X;\phi)\leq t\} is contained in {Δmin(X;ϕ)≤t}\{\Delta_{\min}(X;\phi)\leq t\}. Proposition 3.7 therefore yields constants δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 and Cmargin​(ϕ)>0C_{\mathrm{margin}}(\phi)>0 such that

ℙ⁡(Δ⁡(X,ϕ)≤t)≤Cmargin​(ϕ)​t,0<t≤δ0.\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta(X;\phi)\leq t\bigr)\leq C_{\mathrm{margin}}(\phi)\,t,\qquad 0<t\leq\delta_{0}.

Fix θ\theta and abbreviate hτ:=hθ,ϕ,τh_{\tau}:=h_{\theta,\phi,\tau} and h0:=hθ,ϕ,0h_{0}:=h_{\theta,\phi,0}. Using

(Y−hτ​(X))2−(Y−h0​(X))2=(h0​(X)−hτ​(X))​(2​Y−hτ​(X)−h0​(X)),(Y-h_{\tau}(X))^{2}-(Y-h_{0}(X))^{2}=(h_{0}(X)-h_{\tau}(X))(2Y-h_{\tau}(X)-h_{0}(X)),

together with the bounds |Y|≤BY\left\lvert Y\right\rvert\leq B_{Y} and |hτ​(X)|,|h0​(X)|≤Bf\left\lvert h_{\tau}(X)\right\rvert,\left\lvert h_{0}(X)\right\rvert\leq B_{f}, we obtain

|Lτ​(θ,ϕ)−L0​(θ,ϕ)|≤(2​BY+2​Bf)​𝔼​[|hτ​(X)−h0​(X)|].\left\lvert L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\right\rvert\leq(2B_{Y}+2B_{f})\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\left\lvert h_{\tau}(X)-h_{0}(X)\right\rvert\bigr].

The softmax tail bound then gives

|hτ(x)−h0(x)|≤2Bf(K−1)e−Δ(x;ϕ)/τ.\left\lvert h_{\tau}(x)-h_{0}(x)\right\rvert\leq 2B_{f}(K-1)e^{-\Delta(x;\phi)/\tau}.

Hence

|Lτ(θ,ϕ)−L0(θ,ϕ)|≤4Bf(BY+Bf)(K−1)𝔼[e−Δ(X;ϕ)/τ].\left\lvert L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\right\rvert\leq 4B_{f}(B_{Y}+B_{f})(K-1)\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\Delta(X;\phi)/\tau}\bigr].

Using integration by parts with the distribution function of Δ⁡(X,ϕ)\Delta(X;\phi),

𝔼[e−Δ(X;ϕ)/τ]=1τ∫0∞ℙ(Δ(X;ϕ)≤t)e−t/τdt.\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\Delta(X;\phi)/\tau}\bigr]=\frac{1}{\tau}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Delta(X;\phi)\leq t\bigr)e^{-t/\tau}\,dt.

Split the integral at δ0\delta_{0}. On (0,δ0](0,\delta_{0}] we use the linear bound above, while on [δ0,∞)[\delta_{0},\infty) we use ℙ⁡(Δ≤t)≤1\mathbb{P}(\Delta\leq t)\leq 1. This gives

𝔼[e−Δ(X;ϕ)/τ]≤Cmargin​(ϕ)τ∫0δ0te−t/τdt+e−δ0/τ≤Cmargin(ϕ)τ+e−δ0/τ.\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\Delta(X;\phi)/\tau}\bigr]\leq\frac{C_{\mathrm{margin}}(\phi)}{\tau}\int_{0}^{\delta_{0}}te^{-t/\tau}\,dt+e^{-\delta_{0}/\tau}\leq C_{\mathrm{margin}}(\phi)\tau+e^{-\delta_{0}/\tau}.

Choose τ0>0\tau_{0}>0 so that e−δ0/τ≤τe^{-\delta_{0}/\tau}\leq\tau for all τ∈(0,τ0]\tau\in(0,\tau_{0}]. Then

𝔼[e−Δ(X;ϕ)/τ]≤(Cmargin(ϕ)+1)τ,0<τ≤τ0,\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\Delta(X;\phi)/\tau}\bigr]\leq\bigl(C_{\mathrm{margin}}(\phi)+1\bigr)\tau,\qquad 0<\tau\leq\tau_{0},

and the claimed bound follows after absorbing constants into Cco​(ϕ)C_{\mathrm{co}}(\phi). ∎

The next theorem gives the quantitative soft-to-hard approximation used throughout the paper. Its message is straightforward. If the top-two margin has uniformly light tails near zero, then the whole soft family approaches the hard-routing risk at a polynomial rate that is uniform over the parameter set.

Theorem 4.5 (Uniform quantitative soft-to-hard approximation).

Suppose the margin-tail bound (4.4) and Assumption 4.3 hold. Since the margin-tail condition implies that the hard argmax is unique PXP_{X}-almost surely, the hard router is well defined up to a null set. Then there exists a constant Csh>0C_{\mathrm{sh}}>0 (depending only on KK, CC, α\alpha, BYB_{Y} and BfB_{f}) such that for all τ∈(0,1]\tau\in(0,1] and all (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi),

|Lτ​(θ,ϕ)−L0​(θ,ϕ)|≤Csh​τα.\left\lvert L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\right\rvert\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{sh}}\;\tau^{\alpha}.

In particular, Lτ→L0L_{\tau}\to L_{0} uniformly on compact parameter sets, with rate O⁡(τα)O(\tau^{\alpha}).

Proof.

We argue in three short steps. First we reduce the risk difference to the predictor gap hτ−h0h_{\tau}-h_{0}. Then we control that gap with the softmax tail. Finally we integrate against the margin distribution.

We first reduce the risk difference to an L1L^{1} predictor gap. Fix (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) and abbreviate hτ:=hθ,ϕ,τh_{\tau}:=h_{\theta,\phi,\tau} and h0:=hθ,ϕ,0h_{0}:=h_{\theta,\phi,0}. Then

(Y−hτ​(X))2−(Y−h0​(X))2=(h0​(X)−hτ​(X))​(2​Y−hτ​(X)−h0​(X)).(Y-h_{\tau}(X))^{2}-(Y-h_{0}(X))^{2}=(h_{0}(X)-h_{\tau}(X))\bigl(2Y-h_{\tau}(X)-h_{0}(X)\bigr).

Taking absolute values and expectations gives

|Lτ​(θ,ϕ)−L0​(θ,ϕ)|≤𝔼⁡[|hτ​(X)−h0​(X)|​(2​|Y|+|hτ​(X)|+|h0​(X)|)].\left\lvert L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\right\rvert\leq\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\left\lvert h_{\tau}(X)-h_{0}(X)\right\rvert\bigl(2\left\lvert Y\right\rvert+\left\lvert h_{\tau}(X)\right\rvert+\left\lvert h_{0}(X)\right\rvert\bigr)\Bigr]. (4.5)

By Assumption 4.3, |Y|≤BY|Y|\leq B_{Y} and |hτ​(X)|,|h0​(X)|≤Bf|h_{\tau}(X)|,|h_{0}(X)|\leq B_{f} almost surely. Hence

2​|Y|+|hτ​(X)|+|h0​(X)|≤2​BY+2​Bf=:C0,2\left\lvert Y\right\rvert+\left\lvert h_{\tau}(X)\right\rvert+\left\lvert h_{0}(X)\right\rvert\leq 2B_{Y}+2B_{f}=:C_{0},

and therefore

|Lτ​(θ,ϕ)−L0​(θ,ϕ)|≤C0​𝔼​[|hτ​(X)−h0​(X)|].\left\lvert L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\right\rvert\leq C_{0}\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\left\lvert h_{\tau}(X)-h_{0}(X)\right\rvert\bigr]. (4.6)

We next bound hτ−h0h_{\tau}-h_{0} through the score margin. For each xx, let k⋆​(x,ϕ)k^{\star}(x;\phi) be the unique maximizer of ak​(x,ϕ)a_{k}(x;\phi); this is defined PXP_{X}-almost surely by assumption. Then

hτ​(x)=∑k=1Kpk(τ)​(x,ϕ)​fk​(x,θk),h0​(x)=fk⋆​(x,ϕ)​(x,θk⋆​(x,ϕ)).h_{\tau}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)f_{k}(x;\theta_{k}),\qquad h_{0}(x)=f_{k^{\star}(x;\phi)}(x;\theta_{k^{\star}(x;\phi)}).

Subtracting and using ∑kpk(τ)​(x,ϕ)=1\sum_{k}p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)=1 gives

hτ​(x)−h0​(x)=∑k≠k⋆​(x,ϕ)pk(τ)​(x,ϕ)​(fk​(x,θk)−fk⋆​(x,ϕ)​(x,θk⋆​(x,ϕ))).h_{\tau}(x)-h_{0}(x)=\sum_{k\neq k^{\star}(x;\phi)}p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\bigl(f_{k}(x;\theta_{k})-f_{k^{\star}(x;\phi)}(x;\theta_{k^{\star}(x;\phi)})\bigr).

Since |fk|≤Bf|f_{k}|\leq B_{f}, we obtain the pointwise estimate

|hτ​(x)−h0​(x)|≤2​Bf​∑k≠k⋆​(x,ϕ)pk(τ)​(x,ϕ)=2​Bf​(1−pk⋆​(x,ϕ)(τ)​(x,ϕ)).\left\lvert h_{\tau}(x)-h_{0}(x)\right\rvert\leq 2B_{f}\sum_{k\neq k^{\star}(x;\phi)}p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)=2B_{f}\bigl(1-p_{k^{\star}(x;\phi)}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\bigr). (4.7)

Now sort the logits at xx as z(1)≥z(2)≥⋯≥z(K)z_{(1)}\geq z_{(2)}\geq\cdots\geq z_{(K)}. By Lemma 4.1,

1−pk⋆​(x,ϕ)(τ)(x;ϕ)≤(K−1)exp(−(z(1)−z(2))/τ)=(K−1)exp(−Δ(x;ϕ)/τ).1-p_{k^{\star}(x;\phi)}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\leq(K-1)\exp\bigl(-(z_{(1)}-z_{(2)})/\tau\bigr)=(K-1)\exp\bigl(-\Delta(x;\phi)/\tau\bigr).

Combining this with (4.7),

|hτ(x)−h0(x)|≤2Bf(K−1)exp(−Δ(x;ϕ)/τ).\left\lvert h_{\tau}(x)-h_{0}(x)\right\rvert\leq 2B_{f}(K-1)\exp\bigl(-\Delta(x;\phi)/\tau\bigr).

After taking expectations we arrive at

𝔼[|hτ(X)−h0(X)|]≤2Bf(K−1)𝔼[exp(−Δ(X;ϕ)/τ)].\mathbb{E}\bigl[\left\lvert h_{\tau}(X)-h_{0}(X)\right\rvert\bigr]\leq 2B_{f}(K-1)\mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp\bigl(-\Delta(X;\phi)/\tau\bigr)\bigr]. (4.8)

We now integrate the margin-tail bound. Let Fϕ​(t):=ℙ⁡(Δ⁡(X,ϕ)≤t)F_{\phi}(t):=\mathbb{P}(\Delta(X;\phi)\leq t). By the margin-tail bound (4.4),

Fϕ​(t)≤C​tα,t>0,F_{\phi}(t)\leq Ct^{\alpha},\qquad t>0,

uniformly in ϕ\phi. Since Fϕ​(0)=ℙ⁡(Δ=0)=0F_{\phi}(0)=\mathbb{P}(\Delta=0)=0, integration by parts yields

𝔼[e−Δ(X;ϕ)/τ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\Delta(X;\phi)/\tau}\bigr] =∫0∞e−t/τdFϕ(t)\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t/\tau}\,dF_{\phi}(t)
=1τ∫0∞Fϕ(t)e−t/τdt\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\tau}\int_{0}^{\infty}F_{\phi}(t)e^{-t/\tau}\,dt
≤Cτ∫0∞tαe−t/τdt.\displaystyle\leq\frac{C}{\tau}\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{\alpha}e^{-t/\tau}\,dt.

With the substitution t=τ​ut=\tau u we obtain

𝔼[e−Δ(X;ϕ)/τ]≤Cτα∫0∞uαe−udu=CΓ(α+1)τα.\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\Delta(X;\phi)/\tau}\bigr]\leq C\tau^{\alpha}\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{\alpha}e^{-u}\,du=C\Gamma(\alpha+1)\tau^{\alpha}.

Thus there is a constant C1>0C_{1}>0, depending only on CC and α\alpha, such that

𝔼[e−Δ(X;ϕ)/τ]≤C1ταfor all τ∈(0,1] and all ϕ.\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\Delta(X;\phi)/\tau}\bigr]\leq C_{1}\tau^{\alpha}\qquad\text{for all }\tau\in(0,1]\text{ and all }\phi.

Plugging this into (4.8) and then into (4.6) gives

|Lτ​(θ,ϕ)−L0​(θ,ϕ)|≤Csh​τα,\left\lvert L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\right\rvert\leq C_{\mathrm{sh}}\tau^{\alpha},

where CshC_{\mathrm{sh}} depends only on BY,Bf,K,C,B_{Y},B_{f},K,C, and α\alpha. The constants are uniform on compact parameter sets, so the bound is uniform in (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi). ∎

Remark 4.6 (Relation to Γ\Gamma-convergence).

Theorem 4.5 does more than provide the pointwise convergence Lτ→L0L_{\tau}\to L_{0} needed later for Γ\Gamma-convergence. It also gives a uniform polynomial rate on compact parameter sets. That extra uniformity is useful whenever one wants to control the soft–hard approximation over an entire family of parameters, for instance along an annealing trajectory.

4.4 Γ\Gamma-convergence

We equip the parameter space with a product topology that makes (θ,ϕ)↦fk​(⋅,θk)(\theta,\phi)\mapsto f_{k}(\cdot;\theta_{k}) continuous in L2​(PX)L^{2}(P_{X}); for instance, if Θk\Theta_{k} is compact and the map θk↦fk\theta_{k}\mapsto f_{k} is continuous in L2​(PX)L^{2}(P_{X}) for each kk, then the product topology on Θ:=∏kΘk\Theta:=\prod_{k}\Theta_{k} suffices. For the router parameters ϕ\phi we assume a topology such that (θ,ϕ)↦a⁡(⋅,ϕ)(\theta,\phi)\mapsto a(\cdot;\phi) is continuous in L2​(PX)L^{2}(P_{X}) and L∞​(PX)L^{\infty}(P_{X}).

The quantitative soft–hard estimate from Theorem 4.5 is already uniform on compact parameter sets under the margin-tail bound (4.4) and Assumption 4.3. We therefore do not need a separate uniform boundary-mass assumption for the Γ\Gamma-convergence theorem below.

Under these conditions, the limiting statement can be phrased variationally. This is the right level of generality for optimization problems, because it says not only that the soft functionals converge, but also that minimizing sequences cannot lose mass in the limit and must select the hard-routing problem as their asymptotic target.

The next theorem states the zero-temperature limit in the language of minimization. It says that the hard-routing objective is not only a pointwise limit of the soft risks; it is the variational limit selected by their minimizing sequences. Since the margin-tail bound (4.4) gives PX​(Δ⁡(X,ϕ)≤t)≤C​tαP_{X}(\Delta(X;\phi)\leq t)\leq Ct^{\alpha} for every t>0t>0, it also implies PX​(Δ⁡(X,ϕ)=0)=0P_{X}(\Delta(X;\phi)=0)=0 after letting t↓0t\downarrow 0. Thus the hard router is uniquely defined PXP_{X}-almost surely throughout the theorem.

Theorem 4.7 (Variational zero-temperature limit of the soft risks).

Suppose the margin-tail bound (4.4) and Assumption 4.3 hold and the parameter spaces are compact in the topology described above. Then the functionals LτL_{\tau} Γ\Gamma-converge to L0L_{0} on the parameter space as τ→0\tau\to 0. In particular, the following statements hold.

  1. (i)

    (Γ\Gamma-liminf inequality) If (θτ,ϕτ)(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau}) converges to (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) as τ→0\tau\to 0, then

    L0​(θ,ϕ)≤lim infτ→0Lτ​(θτ,ϕτ).L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\leq\liminf_{\tau\to 0}L_{\tau}(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau}).
  2. (ii)

    (Recovery sequence) For every (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) there exists a sequence (θτ,ϕτ)→(θ,ϕ)(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})\to(\theta,\phi) such that

    L0​(θ,ϕ)≥lim supτ→0Lτ​(θτ,ϕτ).L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\geq\limsup_{\tau\to 0}L_{\tau}(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau}).
  3. (iii)

    Any sequence of almost minimizers (θτ,ϕτ)(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau}) with Lτ​(θτ,ϕτ)−infLτ→0L_{\tau}(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})-\inf L_{\tau}\to 0 is precompact, and every cluster point is a minimizer of L0L_{0}.

Proof.

The proof combines the uniform soft-to-hard approximation with continuity of the hard functional. Once those two ingredients are in place, the Γ\Gamma-liminf inequality, the recovery sequence, and the statement about almost minimizers follow directly.

We start from the uniform convergence of LτL_{\tau} to L0L_{0}. Theorem 4.5 already gives a uniform modulus of convergence on compact parameter sets. In particular, there exists a deterministic function ω⁡(τ)↓0\omega(\tau)\downarrow 0 such that

sup(θ,ϕ)|Lτ​(θ,ϕ)−L0​(θ,ϕ)|≤ω⁡(τ).\sup_{(\theta,\phi)}|L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-L_{0}(\theta,\phi)|\leq\omega(\tau). (4.9)

For the present theorem one may take ω⁡(τ)=C​τα\omega(\tau)=C\tau^{\alpha} from Theorem 4.5.

It remains to check continuity of the hard functional L0L_{0} in the chosen topology. Let (θn,ϕn)→(θ,ϕ)(\theta_{n},\phi_{n})\to(\theta,\phi) in the topology described before the theorem. Write

hn​(x):=hθn,ϕn,0​(x),h⁡(x):=hθ,ϕ,0​(x).h_{n}(x):=h_{\theta_{n},\phi_{n},0}(x),\qquad h(x):=h_{\theta,\phi,0}(x).

We claim that hn→hh_{n}\to h in L1​(PX)L^{1}(P_{X}), which will imply L0​(θn,ϕn)→L0​(θ,ϕ)L_{0}(\theta_{n},\phi_{n})\to L_{0}(\theta,\phi).

Set

δn:=max1≤k≤K⁡‖ak​(⋅,ϕn)−ak​(⋅,ϕ)‖L∞​(PX)→n→∞0.\delta_{n}:=\max_{1\leq k\leq K}\|a_{k}(\cdot;\phi_{n})-a_{k}(\cdot;\phi)\|_{L^{\infty}(P_{X})}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0.

Define the stable region

An:={x:Δ⁡(x,ϕ)>2​δn}.A_{n}:=\{x:\Delta(x;\phi)>2\delta_{n}\}.

On AnA_{n}, the maximizer of the logits is unchanged when ϕ\phi is replaced by ϕn\phi_{n}. Indeed, if k⋆​(x,ϕ)k^{\star}(x;\phi) is the unique winner for ϕ\phi, then every competing logit remains at least Δ⁡(x,ϕ)−2​δn>0\Delta(x;\phi)-2\delta_{n}>0 below it under the perturbation. Hence on AnA_{n} the hard router selects the same expert for hnh_{n} and hh, and therefore

|hn(x)−h(x)|≤∑k=1K|fk(x;θn,k)−fk(x;θk)| 1{k⋆(x;ϕ)=k}.|h_{n}(x)-h(x)|\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}|f_{k}(x;\theta_{n,k})-f_{k}(x;\theta_{k})|\,\mathbf{1}_{\{k^{\star}(x;\phi)=k\}}.

Taking expectations and using L2​(PX)L^{2}(P_{X})-continuity of each expert map,

𝔼⁡[|hn−h|​𝟏An]≤∑k=1K‖fk​(⋅,θn,k)−fk​(⋅,θk)‖L1​(PX)→n→∞0.\mathbb{E}\bigl[|h_{n}-h|\mathbf{1}_{A_{n}}\bigr]\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|f_{k}(\cdot;\theta_{n,k})-f_{k}(\cdot;\theta_{k})\|_{L^{1}(P_{X})}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0. (4.10)

On the complement Anc={Δ(X;ϕ)≤2δn}A_{n}^{c}=\{\Delta(X;\phi)\leq 2\delta_{n}\}, the hard predictions may differ because the winner can switch, but this set is small. Indeed, the margin-tail bound (4.4) gives

PX​(Anc)≤C​(2​δn)αP_{X}(A_{n}^{c})\leq C\,(2\delta_{n})^{\alpha}

for all large nn, and |hn|,|h|≤Bf|h_{n}|,|h|\leq B_{f}. Therefore

𝔼⁡[|hn−h|​𝟏Anc]≤2​Bf​PX​(Anc)≤2α+1​Bf​C​δnα→n→∞0.\mathbb{E}\bigl[|h_{n}-h|\mathbf{1}_{A_{n}^{c}}\bigr]\leq 2B_{f}\,P_{X}(A_{n}^{c})\leq 2^{\alpha+1}B_{f}C\,\delta_{n}^{\alpha}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0. (4.11)

Combining (4.10) and (4.11) yields hn→hh_{n}\to h in L1​(PX)L^{1}(P_{X}). Since |Y|≤BY|Y|\leq B_{Y} and |hn|,|h|≤Bf|h_{n}|,|h|\leq B_{f},

|(Y−hn)2−(Y−h)2|≤2​(BY+Bf)​|hn−h|,\bigl|(Y-h_{n})^{2}-(Y-h)^{2}\bigr|\leq 2(B_{Y}+B_{f})|h_{n}-h|,

so L0​(θn,ϕn)→L0​(θ,ϕ)L_{0}(\theta_{n},\phi_{n})\to L_{0}(\theta,\phi). Thus L0L_{0} is continuous.

We can now verify Γ\Gamma-convergence and identify the behavior of almost minimizers. Let (θτ,ϕτ)→(θ,ϕ)(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})\to(\theta,\phi). From (4.9),

Lτ​(θτ,ϕτ)≥L0​(θτ,ϕτ)−ω⁡(τ).L_{\tau}(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})\geq L_{0}(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})-\omega(\tau).

Taking lim inf\liminf and using continuity of L0L_{0} gives

lim infτ↓0Lτ​(θτ,ϕτ)≥lim infτ↓0L0​(θτ,ϕτ)=L0​(θ,ϕ),\liminf_{\tau\downarrow 0}L_{\tau}(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})\geq\liminf_{\tau\downarrow 0}L_{0}(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})=L_{0}(\theta,\phi),

which is the Γ\Gamma-liminf inequality.

For the recovery sequence, fix (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) and take the constant sequence (θτ,ϕτ)≡(θ,ϕ)(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})\equiv(\theta,\phi). Then (4.9) gives

lim supτ↓0Lτ​(θτ,ϕτ)≤L0​(θ,ϕ)+lim supτ↓0ω⁡(τ)=L0​(θ,ϕ).\limsup_{\tau\downarrow 0}L_{\tau}(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})\leq L_{0}(\theta,\phi)+\limsup_{\tau\downarrow 0}\omega(\tau)=L_{0}(\theta,\phi).

This proves the recovery property.

Finally, let (θτ,ϕτ)(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau}) be almost minimizers with Lτ​(θτ,ϕτ)−infLτ→0L_{\tau}(\theta_{\tau},\phi_{\tau})-\inf L_{\tau}\to 0. Compactness of the parameter space gives precompactness. Let (θτj,ϕτj)→(θ,ϕ)(\theta_{\tau_{j}},\phi_{\tau_{j}})\to(\theta,\phi) along a subsequence. By the liminf inequality,

L0​(θ,ϕ)≤lim infj→∞Lτj​(θτj,ϕτj).L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\leq\liminf_{j\to\infty}L_{\tau_{j}}(\theta_{\tau_{j}},\phi_{\tau_{j}}).

For any fixed (θ¯,ϕ¯)(\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi}),

Lτj​(θτj,ϕτj)≤Lτj​(θ¯,ϕ¯)+o⁡(1).L_{\tau_{j}}(\theta_{\tau_{j}},\phi_{\tau_{j}})\leq L_{\tau_{j}}(\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi})+o(1).

Passing to the limit and using (4.9) again gives

L0​(θ,ϕ)≤L0​(θ¯,ϕ¯).L_{0}(\theta,\phi)\leq L_{0}(\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi}).

Since (θ¯,ϕ¯)(\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi}) was arbitrary, (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) is a minimizer of L0L_{0}. ∎

5 A conditional landscape-transfer principle at small temperature

This section does not try to prove that mixture-of-experts objectives are generically benign. It shows instead how favorable geometry of a profiled hard-routing problem can be transferred to the soft objective when temperature is small and when the soft objective tracks the hard one to first and second order at boundary-layer scale. This isolates the model-dependent part of the argument from the unconditional geometric core developed earlier.

We write router logits as ak​(x,ϕ)a_{k}(x;\phi) and the associated softmax weights at temperature τ>0\tau>0 as

pk(τ)(x;ϕ):=exp⁡(ak​(x,ϕ)/τ)∑j=1Kexp⁡(aj​(x,ϕ)/τ),k=1,…,K,p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi):=\frac{\exp(a_{k}(x;\phi)/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(a_{j}(x;\phi)/\tau)},\qquad k=1,\dots,K,

and the student prediction as

hθ,ϕ,τ​(x):=fτ​(x,θ,ϕ)=∑k=1Kpk(τ)​(x,ϕ)​fk​(x,θk).h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(x):=f_{\tau}(x;\theta,\phi)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\,f_{k}(x;\theta_{k}).

We begin with the teacher model. We assume a teacher partition (Ωk⋆)k=1K(\Omega_{k}^{\star})_{k=1}^{K} of 𝒳\mathcal{X} (up to ℙ\mathbb{P}-null sets) and teacher experts fk⋆:𝒳→ℝf_{k}^{\star}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}. Given X∼PXX\sim P_{X}, the label is generated by

Y=μ⁡(X)+ξ,𝔼⁡[ξ∣X]=0.Y=\mu(X)+\xi,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\xi\mid X]=0. (5.1)

The teacher signal is the piecewise expert function

μ⁡(x):=∑k=1K𝟙x∈Ωk⋆​fk⋆​(x)(equivalently, ​μ​(x)=fk⋆​(x)​ for ​x∈Ωk⋆​).\mu(x):=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathds{1}_{x\in\Omega_{k}^{\star}}\,f_{k}^{\star}(x)\qquad\text{(equivalently, }\mu(x)=f_{k}^{\star}(x)\text{ for }x\in\Omega_{k}^{\star}\text{).} (5.2)
Assumption 5.1 (Standing teacher–student conditions).

The teacher model (5.1) holds with 𝔼⁡[ξ2]<∞\mathbb{E}[\xi^{2}]<\infty. The sets (Ωk⋆)k=1K(\Omega_{k}^{\star})_{k=1}^{K} form a measurable partition of 𝒳\mathcal{X} up to PXP_{X}-null sets, each fk⋆f_{k}^{\star} is measurable, and there exists B<∞B<\infty such that |μ⁡(X)|≤B\left\lvert\mu(X)\right\rvert\leq B almost surely.

Assumption 5.1 sets up the teacher–student regime used in the rest of the section. Most of it is routine regularity. What really matters is that the teacher supplies a partition and cellwise target experts, so misrouting has a clear population meaning. Outside a teacher–student interpretation, the later statements involving (θ⋆,ϕ⋆)(\theta^{\star},\phi^{\star}) should simply be read relative to a fixed reference decomposition.

We next describe the student model and the integrability conditions needed below. We will use that the teacher experts are representable in the student class and that the student prediction has finite second moment.

Assumption 5.2 (Student realizability and boundedness/moments).

There exist parameters θ⋆=(θ1⋆,…,θK⋆)\theta^{\star}=(\theta_{1}^{\star},\dots,\theta_{K}^{\star}) such that fk​(⋅,θk⋆)=fk⋆​(⋅)f_{k}(\cdot;\theta_{k}^{\star})=f_{k}^{\star}(\cdot) ℙ\mathbb{P}-a.s. on Ωk⋆\Omega_{k}^{\star}. In addition, either the uniform-boundedness branch holds, meaning that there is Bstu<∞B_{\mathrm{stu}}<\infty with supk,x|fk​(x,θk)|≤Bstu\sup_{k,x}\left\lvert f_{k}(x;\theta_{k})\right\rvert\leq B_{\mathrm{stu}} for all parameters under consideration, or the moment-control branch holds, meaning that supk𝔼⁡[|fk​(X,θk)|4]<∞\sup_{k}\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert f_{k}(X;\theta_{k})\right\rvert^{4}]<\infty and hence 𝔼⁡[hθ,ϕ,τ​(X)2]<∞\mathbb{E}[h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X)^{2}]<\infty for all (θ,ϕ,τ)(\theta,\phi,\tau).

Assumption 5.2 does two different jobs. One part says that the student class can realize the teacher experts on their own cells. The other part gives the boundedness or moment control needed for exchanging expectations and derivatives and for keeping the remainder terms finite. Uniform boundedness is natural for bounded-output experts or after explicit clipping, while moment assumptions are the right substitute when the outputs are unbounded but still have controlled tails.

In applications this type of control is often enforced only indirectly, through regularization and clipping. If the training dynamics produce rare but extremely large losses or gradients, then one should expect the present boundary-mass bounds to become correspondingly crude.

Assumption 5.3 (Teacher-router realizability and interface regularity).

There exists a router parameter ϕ⋆\phi^{\star} such that the hard partition induced by the logits ak​(⋅,ϕ⋆)a_{k}(\cdot;\phi^{\star}) agrees with the teacher partition (Ωk⋆)k=1K(\Omega_{k}^{\star})_{k=1}^{K} up to PXP_{X}-null sets. For each adjacent teacher pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell), the corresponding teacher interface

𝒮k​ℓ⋆:=∂Ωk⋆∩∂Ωℓ⋆\mathcal{S}_{k\ell}^{\star}:=\partial\Omega_{k}^{\star}\cap\partial\Omega_{\ell}^{\star}

is, away from multiway junctions (that is, points where three or more routing cells meet), a compact C2C^{2} hypersurface on which ∇(ak−aℓ)​(x,ϕ⋆)≠0\nabla(a_{k}-a_{\ell})(x;\phi^{\star})\neq 0. In addition, pXp_{X} is bounded on a neighborhood of the union of the teacher interfaces, and the pairwise score differences Sk​ℓ​(⋅,ϕ⋆)S_{k\ell}(\cdot;\phi^{\star}) satisfy the tubular coarea regularity of Assumption 3.4 on the teacher-router interfaces.

Assumption 5.3 supplies the reference router that is used later when comparing a global minimizer to the teacher configuration. It also gives the regularity needed to define the teacher-side normals and traces and, by explicitly invoking Assumption 3.4 at ϕ⋆\phi^{\star}, to apply the linear boundary-mass estimate at the teacher router.

The student MoE uses the same number of experts KK, with parameters (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) and temperature τ\tau. We think of τ\tau as small but positive; in the limit τ→0\tau\to 0 the router becomes hard and the model approaches a piecewise-expert model with moving boundaries.

5.1 Risk decomposition: interior vs boundary tubes

The population risk (2.1) can be decomposed by conditioning on XX.

Lτ​(θ,ϕ)=𝔼⁡[(Y−hθ,ϕ,τ​(X))2]=𝔼⁡[(μ⁡(X)−hθ,ϕ,τ​(X))2]+𝔼⁡[ξ2].L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(Y-h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X))^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mu(X)-h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X))^{2}\bigr]+\mathbb{E}[\xi^{2}].

The noise variance 𝔼⁡[ξ2]\mathbb{E}[\xi^{2}] is independent of (θ,ϕ,τ)(\theta,\phi,\tau), so we focus on

L~τ​(θ,ϕ):=𝔼⁡[(μ⁡(X)−hθ,ϕ,τ​(X))2].\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta,\phi):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mu(X)-h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X))^{2}\bigr].

For a fixed ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2), router parameter ϕ\phi, and temperature τ>0\tau>0, define the KK-way ambiguity region

𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ):={x∈𝒳:max1≤k≤K⁡pk(τ)​(x,ϕ)≤1−ε},𝒢ε​(τ,ϕ):=𝒳∖𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ).\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi):=\Bigl\{x\in\mathcal{X}:\ \max_{1\leq k\leq K}p_{k}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\leq 1-\varepsilon\Bigr\},\qquad\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi):=\mathcal{X}\setminus\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi). (5.3)

Thus on 𝒢ε​(τ,ϕ)\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi) there exists (at least one) expert with routing weight at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon.

We also need the boundary mass induced by the router. Define the router-dependent boundary-mass quantity

BMϕ​(τ,ε):=ℙ⁡(X∈𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ)).\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon):=\mathbb{P}\bigl(X\in\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\bigr). (5.4)
Remark 5.4 (Relation to earlier boundary-mass notions).

The notation becomes lighter if one keeps the roles of the various quantities separate. The top–two margin Δ⁡(X,ϕ)\Delta(X;\phi) is the most direct measure of soft-versus-hard ambiguity, because the softmax weights are controlled by the gap between the winning and second-best logits. The pairwise quantity Δmin​(X,ϕ)\Delta_{\min}(X;\phi) is slightly larger but geometrically easier to estimate, since it describes a union of pairwise slabs around the surfaces {ak=aℓ}\{a_{k}=a_{\ell}\}. Finally, BMϕ​(τ,ε)\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon) is not a new geometric object; it is the probability of the temperature-dependent ambiguity event 𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ)\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi), hence a rescaled version of the same small-margin region.

Let

κε:=log⁡(1−εε),κε,K:=log⁡((K−1)​(1−ε)ε).\kappa_{\varepsilon}:=\log\!\Bigl(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Bigr),\qquad\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}:=\log\!\Bigl(\frac{(K-1)(1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\Bigr).

Then for every τ>0\tau>0,

{Δ(X;ϕ)≤κετ}⊆{X∈𝒰ε(τ;ϕ)}⊆{Δ(X;ϕ)≤κε,Kτ}.\bigl\{\Delta(X;\phi)\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon}\,\tau\bigr\}\subseteq\bigl\{X\in\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\bigr\}\subseteq\bigl\{\Delta(X;\phi)\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\,\tau\bigr\}.

Equivalently, in terms of the boundary-mass profiles introduced in Section 2,

BMϕtop​(κε​τ)≤BMϕ​(τ,ε)≤BMϕtop​(κε,K​τ)≤BMϕpair​(κε,K​τ).\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{top}}_{\phi}(\kappa_{\varepsilon}\,\tau)\leq\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon)\leq\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{top}}_{\phi}(\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\,\tau)\leq\mathrm{BM}^{\mathrm{pair}}_{\phi}(\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\,\tau).

Thus the later estimates can be read in whichever language is most convenient. Top–two margins describe softmax tails, pairwise slabs support the coarea arguments, and 𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ)\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi) is the set used in the actual decomposition of the risk. In particular, for K=2K=2 we have κε,K=κε\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}=\kappa_{\varepsilon} and the ambiguity event reduces to the familiar binary slab condition.

Lemma 5.5 (Risk decomposition).

Under Assumption 5.1 and the uniform boundedness alternative in the uniform-boundedness branch of Assumption 5.2, for any ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2),

L~τ​(θ,ϕ)=L~τ,int​(θ,ϕ)+L~τ,bdry​(θ,ϕ),\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)=\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{int}}(\theta,\phi)+\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{bdry}}(\theta,\phi),

where

L~τ,int​(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{int}}(\theta,\phi) :=𝔼⁡[(μ⁡(X)−hθ,ϕ,τ​(X))2|X∈𝒢ε​(τ,ϕ)]​ℙ​(X∈𝒢ε​(τ,ϕ)),\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mu(X)-h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X))^{2}\,\big|\,X\in\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\bigr]\,\mathbb{P}\bigl(X\in\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\bigr),
L~τ,bdry​(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{bdry}}(\theta,\phi) :=𝔼⁡[(μ⁡(X)−hθ,ϕ,τ​(X))2|X∈𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ)]​ℙ​(X∈𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ)).\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mu(X)-h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X))^{2}\,\big|\,X\in\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\bigr]\,\mathbb{P}\bigl(X\in\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\bigr).

Moreover, there exists a constant C⁡(ε,B,Bstu)C(\varepsilon,B,B_{\mathrm{stu}}) such that

0≤L~τ,bdry​(θ,ϕ)≤C⁡(ε,B,Bstu)​BMϕ​(τ,ε),0\leq\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{bdry}}(\theta,\phi)\leq C(\varepsilon,B,B_{\mathrm{stu}})\,\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon),

for all (θ,ϕ,τ)(\theta,\phi,\tau).

Proof.

We split the expectation over 𝒢ε​(τ,ϕ)\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi) and 𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ)\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi).

L~τ(θ,ϕ)=𝔼[(μ(X)−h(X))2]=𝔼[(μ(X)−h(X))2𝟙{X∈𝒢ε(τ;ϕ)}]+𝔼[(μ(X)−h(X))2𝟙{X∈𝒰ε(τ;ϕ)}],\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mu(X)-h(X))^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mu(X)-h(X))^{2}\mathds{1}_{\{X\in\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\}}\bigr]+\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mu(X)-h(X))^{2}\mathds{1}_{\{X\in\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\}}\bigr],

where we abbreviate h=hθ,ϕ,τh=h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}, and then factor each term as a conditional expectation times the corresponding probability.

For the upper bound on the boundary term, on 𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ)\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi) we have (μ−h)2≤2​μ2+2​h2(\mu-h)^{2}\leq 2\mu^{2}+2h^{2}. the boundedness part of Assumption 5.1 gives |μ⁡(X)|≤B\left\lvert\mu(X)\right\rvert\leq B a.s. On the other hand, h⁡(X)=∑k=1Kpk​(X)​fk​(X,θk)h(X)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}(X)f_{k}(X;\theta_{k}) and ∑kpk​(X)=1\sum_{k}p_{k}(X)=1, so the uniform boundedness hypothesis in the uniform-boundedness branch of Assumption 5.2 yields |h⁡(X)|≤Bstu\left\lvert h(X)\right\rvert\leq B_{\mathrm{stu}} a.s. Therefore

(μ⁡(X)−h⁡(X))2≤2​B2+2​Bstu2a.s.(\mu(X)-h(X))^{2}\leq 2B^{2}+2B_{\mathrm{stu}}^{2}\qquad\text{a.s.}

and hence

L~τ,bdry​(θ,ϕ)≤(2​B2+2​Bstu2)​ℙ​(X∈𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ))=(2​B2+2​Bstu2)​BMϕ​(τ,ε).\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{bdry}}(\theta,\phi)\leq(2B^{2}+2B_{\mathrm{stu}}^{2})\,\mathbb{P}(X\in\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi))=(2B^{2}+2B_{\mathrm{stu}}^{2})\,\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon).
