Remark 5.6 (Why the moment-only alternative is not used here).

A global fourth-moment bound is enough to ensure that L~τ​(θ,ϕ)\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta,\phi) is finite, but it does not by itself yield a uniform bound on conditional second moments over the shrinking ambiguity regions 𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ)\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi). The linear boundary-layer estimate above therefore uses the bounded-output regime. A moment-only version would require an additional localized integrability hypothesis on those ambiguity sets.

Thus the contribution of the boundary tubes to the risk is controlled by the boundary mass. For small τ\tau, the next lemma gives BMϕ​(τ,ε)=O⁡(τ)\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon)=O(\tau) under mild regularity, so the boundary term is O⁡(τ)O(\tau) as well.

Lemma 5.7 (Linear boundary-mass scaling under regularity).

Suppose the fixed router parameter ϕ\phi satisfies the pairwise tubular coarea regularity of Assumption 3.4. Then for each fixed ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2) there is Cε<∞C_{\varepsilon}<\infty such that for all τ\tau sufficiently small,

BMϕ​(τ,ε)≤Cε​τ.\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon)\leq C_{\varepsilon}\tau.
Proof.

By Remark 5.4, the KK-way ambiguity event is contained in a finite union of pairwise slabs:

{X∈𝒰ε(τ;ϕ)}\displaystyle\{X\in\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\} ⊆{Δ(X;ϕ)≤κε,Kτ}\displaystyle\subseteq\{\Delta(X;\phi)\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\tau\}
⊆{Δmin(X;ϕ)≤κε,Kτ}\displaystyle\subseteq\{\Delta_{\min}(X;\phi)\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\tau\}
=⋃1≤k<ℓ≤K{|ak(X;ϕ)−aℓ(X;ϕ)|≤κε,Kτ}.\displaystyle=\bigcup_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}\bigl\{|a_{k}(X;\phi)-a_{\ell}(X;\phi)|\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\tau\bigr\}.

Therefore,

BMϕ​(τ,ε)≤∑1≤k<ℓ≤Kℙ⁡(|Sk​ℓ​(X,ϕ)|≤κε,K​τ).\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon)\leq\sum_{1\leq k<\ell\leq K}\mathbb{P}\bigl(|S_{k\ell}(X;\phi)|\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\tau\bigr).

By the coarea formula and the level-set profile bound from Assumption 3.4,

ℙ(|Sk​ℓ(X;ϕ)|≤κε,Kτ)=∫−κε,K​τκε,K​τ∫{Sk​ℓ(⋅;ϕ)=t}pX​(x)‖∇xSk​ℓ​(x,ϕ)‖dℋd−1(x)dt≤Ck​ℓ(ε)τ,\mathbb{P}\bigl(|S_{k\ell}(X;\phi)|\leq\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\tau\bigr)=\int_{-\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\tau}^{\kappa_{\varepsilon,K}\tau}\int_{\{S_{k\ell}(\cdot;\phi)=t\}}\frac{p_{X}(x)}{\|\nabla_{x}S_{k\ell}(x;\phi)\|}\,d\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x)\,dt\leq C_{k\ell}(\varepsilon)\,\tau,

where Ck​ℓ​(ε)C_{k\ell}(\varepsilon) is finite by the level-set profile bound in Assumption 3.4. Summing over k<ℓk<\ell gives BMϕ​(τ,ε)≤Cε​τ\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon)\leq C_{\varepsilon}\tau for a finite constant CεC_{\varepsilon}. ∎

5.2 Error control on correctly dominated interiors

Inside a teacher cell Ωk⋆\Omega_{k}^{\star}, the router ideally assigns almost all mass to expert kk. In this regime, the MoE behaves like a single-expert model, and a pointwise quadratic comparison controls the error of fk​(⋅,θk)f_{k}(\cdot;\theta_{k}) on the correctly dominated interior.

Proposition 5.8 (Cellwise error control on the correctly dominated interior).

Fix kk and define

Ak,ε(θ,ϕ,τ):=Ωk⋆∩𝒢ε(τ;ϕ)∩{pk(τ)(X;ϕ)≥1−ε}.A_{k,\varepsilon}(\theta,\phi,\tau):=\Omega_{k}^{\star}\cap\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\cap\{p_{k}^{(\tau)}(X;\phi)\geq 1-\varepsilon\}.

Under Assumption 5.1 and the uniform boundedness alternative in the uniform-boundedness branch of Assumption 5.2,

𝔼⁡[(μ⁡(X)−hθ,ϕ,τ​(X))2​ 1Ak,ε​(θ,ϕ,τ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl(\mu(X)-h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X)\bigr)^{2}\,\mathds{1}_{A_{k,\varepsilon}(\theta,\phi,\tau)}\Bigr]
≥12​𝔼​[|fk​(X,θk)−fk⋆​(X)|2​ 1Ak,ε​(θ,ϕ,τ)]−4​Bstu2​ε2​PX​(Ak,ε​(θ,ϕ,τ)).\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\left\lvert f_{k}(X;\theta_{k})-f_{k}^{\star}(X)\right\rvert^{2}\,\mathds{1}_{A_{k,\varepsilon}(\theta,\phi,\tau)}\Bigr]-4B_{\mathrm{stu}}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}\,P_{X}\bigl(A_{k,\varepsilon}(\theta,\phi,\tau)\bigr).

Write

hθ,ϕ,τ​(X)=pk(τ)​(X,ϕ)​fk​(X,θk)+∑ℓ≠kpℓ(τ)​(X,ϕ)​fℓ​(X,θℓ).h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X)=p_{k}^{(\tau)}(X;\phi)\,f_{k}(X;\theta_{k})+\sum_{\ell\neq k}p_{\ell}^{(\tau)}(X;\phi)\,f_{\ell}(X;\theta_{\ell}).

Then

fk⋆​(X)−hθ,ϕ,τ​(X)=(fk⋆​(X)−fk​(X,θk))+((1−pk(τ)​(X,ϕ))​fk​(X,θk)−∑ℓ≠kpℓ(τ)​(X,ϕ)​fℓ​(X,θℓ)).f_{k}^{\star}(X)-h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X)=\bigl(f_{k}^{\star}(X)-f_{k}(X;\theta_{k})\bigr)+\Bigl((1-p_{k}^{(\tau)}(X;\phi))f_{k}(X;\theta_{k})-\sum_{\ell\neq k}p_{\ell}^{(\tau)}(X;\phi)\,f_{\ell}(X;\theta_{\ell})\Bigr).

Using (a+b)2≥12​a2−b2(a+b)^{2}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}a^{2}-b^{2} with a=fk⋆​(X)−fk​(X,θk)a=f_{k}^{\star}(X)-f_{k}(X;\theta_{k}) and bb equal to the remaining parenthesis, we get

(fk⋆​(X)−hθ,ϕ,τ​(X))2≥12​|fk⋆​(X)−fk​(X,θk)|2−|b|2.(f_{k}^{\star}(X)-h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(X))^{2}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\,\left\lvert f_{k}^{\star}(X)-f_{k}(X;\theta_{k})\right\rvert^{2}-\left\lvert b\right\rvert^{2}.

|b|≤(1−pk(τ)​(X,ϕ))​|fk​(X,θk)|+∑ℓ≠kpℓ(τ)​(X,ϕ)​|fℓ​(X,θℓ)|≤2​ε​Bstu.\left\lvert b\right\rvert\leq(1-p_{k}^{(\tau)}(X;\phi))\left\lvert f_{k}(X;\theta_{k})\right\rvert+\sum_{\ell\neq k}p_{\ell}^{(\tau)}(X;\phi)\left\lvert f_{\ell}(X;\theta_{\ell})\right\rvert\leq 2\varepsilon B_{\mathrm{stu}}.

Remark 5.9 (Moment-only variants).

The unconditional form above is chosen so that no conditional L2L^{2} estimate on Ak,εA_{k,\varepsilon} is needed. A version based only on fourth moments would again require extra localized integrability on the events where the router is nearly deterministic.

5.3 Shape derivatives and strict saddles

We now describe how to perturb the router partition and compute the resulting change in risk via shape derivatives [5, 9]. The key idea is that moving a router boundary across regions where one expert is strictly better than another must decrease the risk, yielding a descent direction; under a suitable nondegeneracy condition, this produces a strict-saddle direction.

Consider a fixed pair of neighboring cells (Ωk,Ωℓ)(\Omega_{k},\Omega_{\ell}) separated by a smooth interface 𝒮k​ℓ\mathcal{S}_{k\ell} with outward normal nk​ℓn_{k\ell} pointing from Ωk\Omega_{k} into Ωℓ\Omega_{\ell}. A normal deformation of the interface is specified by a smooth scalar field φ:𝒮k​ℓ→ℝ\varphi:\mathcal{S}_{k\ell}\to\mathbb{R}. Points on 𝒮k​ℓ\mathcal{S}_{k\ell} are pushed along the normal by ϵ​φ​(x)​nk​ℓ​(x)\epsilon\varphi(x)n_{k\ell}(x) for small ϵ\epsilon. This induces a family of perturbed domains (Ωkϵ,Ωℓϵ)(\Omega_{k}^{\epsilon},\Omega_{\ell}^{\epsilon}) and hence a perturbed partition (Ωjϵ)j=1K(\Omega_{j}^{\epsilon})_{j=1}^{K}.

Define the loss contrast

Dk​ℓ​(x,θ,μ):=(fk​(x,θk)−μ⁡(x))2−(fℓ​(x,θℓ)−μ⁡(x))2.D_{k\ell}(x;\theta,\mu):=\bigl(f_{k}(x;\theta_{k})-\mu(x)\bigr)^{2}-\bigl(f_{\ell}(x;\theta_{\ell})-\mu(x)\bigr)^{2}. (5.5)

This notation is kept separate from the routing margin Δ⁡(x,ϕ)\Delta(x;\phi) in (2.4). The quantity Dk​ℓ​(x,θ,μ)D_{k\ell}(x;\theta,\mu) measures how much worse expert kk is compared to expert ℓ\ell at point xx when the target is μ⁡(x)\mu(x).

Proposition 5.10 (Localized shape derivative of risk).

Suppose Assumption 5.1 holds, and fix an adjacent pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell) for the induced hard partition. Let 𝒫⋐𝒮k​ℓ\mathcal{P}\Subset\mathcal{S}_{k\ell} be a relatively compact C2C^{2} patch of the interface whose closure stays away from all multiway junctions. Assume that pXp_{X} has a continuous trace on 𝒫\mathcal{P} and that the teacher signal μ\mu admits one-sided traces on 𝒫\mathcal{P} from Ωk\Omega_{k} and Ωℓ\Omega_{\ell}; this holds, for example, when the corresponding teacher experts extend continuously to the patch from their respective sides. Consider a normal deformation of 𝒫\mathcal{P} given by a smooth compactly supported field φ∈Cc∞​(𝒫)\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{P}), and write φ+:=max⁡{φ,0}\varphi_{+}:=\max\{\varphi,0\} and φ−:=max⁡{−φ,0}\varphi_{-}:=\max\{-\varphi,0\}. Let μk\mu_{k} and μℓ\mu_{\ell} denote the one-sided traces of μ\mu on 𝒫\mathcal{P} from Ωk\Omega_{k} and Ωℓ\Omega_{\ell}, respectively. Then the first variation of the hard-routing risk

L~0​(θ,ϕ):=𝔼⁡[(μ⁡(X)−hθ,ϕ,0​(X))2]\widetilde{L}_{0}(\theta,\phi):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\mu(X)-h_{\theta,\phi,0}(X))^{2}\bigr]

with respect to this localized two-phase deformation is

dd​ϵ​L~0​(θ,ϕϵ)|ϵ=0=∫𝒫[φ+​(x)​Dk​ℓ​(x,θ,μℓ)−φ−​(x)​Dk​ℓ​(x,θ,μk)]​pX​(x)​d​ℋd−1​(x).\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\epsilon}\widetilde{L}_{0}(\theta,\phi_{\epsilon})\biggr|_{\epsilon=0}=\int_{\mathcal{P}}\Bigl[\varphi_{+}(x)\,D_{k\ell}(x;\theta,\mu_{\ell})-\varphi_{-}(x)\,D_{k\ell}(x;\theta,\mu_{k})\Bigr]p_{X}(x)\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x). (5.6)

In particular, if φ≥0\varphi\geq 0 on 𝒫\mathcal{P}, this reduces to

dd​ϵ​L~0​(θ,ϕϵ)|ϵ=0=∫𝒫φ⁡(x)​Dk​ℓ​(x,θ,μℓ)​pX​(x)​d​ℋd−1​(x),\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\epsilon}\widetilde{L}_{0}(\theta,\phi_{\epsilon})\biggr|_{\epsilon=0}=\int_{\mathcal{P}}\varphi(x)\,D_{k\ell}(x;\theta,\mu_{\ell})\,p_{X}(x)\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x),

and if φ≤0\varphi\leq 0 on 𝒫\mathcal{P}, it becomes

dd​ϵ​L~0​(θ,ϕϵ)|ϵ=0=∫𝒫φ⁡(x)​Dk​ℓ​(x,θ,μk)​pX​(x)​d​ℋd−1​(x).\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\epsilon}\widetilde{L}_{0}(\theta,\phi_{\epsilon})\biggr|_{\epsilon=0}=\int_{\mathcal{P}}\varphi(x)\,D_{k\ell}(x;\theta,\mu_{k})\,p_{X}(x)\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(x).

Moreover, if the first variation vanishes for a nonzero realized velocity and the corresponding localized second shape derivative is strictly negative, then the hard-routing objective has a negative-curvature direction along that localized two-phase deformation.

Proof.

Because the deformation is supported on a smooth patch 𝒫\mathcal{P} away from multiway junctions, the problem is locally two-phase and the standard Hadamard–Zolésio transport formula applies; see, for example, [9, Chs. 2–3] or [5, Ch. 5]. Write the hard risk locally as

J⁡(ϵ)=∫ΩkϵFk​(x)​pX​(x)​𝑑x+∫ΩℓϵFℓ​(x)​pX​(x)​𝑑x,Fj​(x):=(μ⁡(x)−fj​(x,θj))2,J(\epsilon)=\int_{\Omega_{k}^{\epsilon}}F_{k}(x)\,p_{X}(x)\,dx+\int_{\Omega_{\ell}^{\epsilon}}F_{\ell}(x)\,p_{X}(x)\,dx,\qquad F_{j}(x):=(\mu(x)-f_{j}(x;\theta_{j}))^{2},

with all other cells unchanged. When φ⁡(x)>0\varphi(x)>0, the interface moves in the normal direction from Ωk\Omega_{k} into Ωℓ\Omega_{\ell}, so Ωk\Omega_{k} gains an infinitesimal layer that originally belonged to Ωℓ\Omega_{\ell}. The transported target on that layer is therefore the Ωℓ\Omega_{\ell}-trace μℓ\mu_{\ell}, and the jump contribution is Dk​ℓ​(x,θ,μℓ)D_{k\ell}(x;\theta,\mu_{\ell}). Likewise, when φ⁡(x)<0\varphi(x)<0, the phase Ωk\Omega_{k} loses an infinitesimal layer to Ωℓ\Omega_{\ell}, so the relevant trace is μk\mu_{k} and the contribution is Dk​ℓ​(x,θ,μk)D_{k\ell}(x;\theta,\mu_{k}) multiplied by the negative velocity. Splitting φ=φ+−φ−\varphi=\varphi_{+}-\varphi_{-} therefore gives (5.6).

The final claim is the usual second-order consequence of the shape calculation. If the first variation vanishes and the second shape derivative is strictly negative along a realized deformation, then the hard objective decreases to second order along that deformation, so the corresponding quadratic form is negative. ∎

Thus, on any smooth two-phase patch away from junctions, a vanishing first variation together with strictly negative second variation yields a genuine local shape descent direction. To transfer this to the parameter variable ϕ\phi, we will only need a realizability condition ensuring that the router can produce the finite-dimensional family of interface velocities that actually arise from its own parameterization.

5.4 Global minima and strict saddles under the transfer assumptions

We now combine the previous ingredients. At this stage one could impose a stronger pointwise contrast condition along teacher interfaces, but the main theorem below does not need that level of separation. For the argument actually used in this paper, the weaker probabilistic specialization-gap condition stated next is enough.

Assumption 5.11 (Probabilistic specialization gap (no large “expert cloning”)).

There exist constants γgap>0\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}>0 and ηgap∈[0,1)\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}\in[0,1) such that for every pair k≠ℓk\neq\ell,

supθℓ∈ΘℓPX​({x∈Ωk⋆:(fℓ​(x,θℓ)−fk⋆​(x))2≤γgap})≤ηgap.\sup_{\theta_{\ell}\in\Theta_{\ell}}\;P_{X}\Bigl(\bigl\{x\in\Omega_{k}^{\star}:\ (f_{\ell}(x;\theta_{\ell})-f_{k}^{\star}(x))^{2}\leq\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}\bigr\}\Bigr)\leq\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}.

Thus a wrong expert may imitate the correct teacher expert on a small exceptional subset of Ωk⋆\Omega_{k}^{\star}, but not on a set of non-negligible probability mass.

Assumption 5.11 rules out large-scale expert collapse. In the extreme case ηgap=0\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}=0, it says that a wrong expert cannot match the correct teacher expert on a set of positive measure inside the wrong cell.

We also require router realizability of normal deformations. To connect shape-derivative directions to actual parameter directions, we use the following notation and hypothesis.

Assumption 5.12 (Router regularity and realized interface directions).

The router logits ak​(⋅,ϕ)a_{k}(\cdot;\phi) are C2C^{2} in xx and C2C^{2} in ϕ\phi. For each operating point ϕ\phi, each adjacent pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell), and each smooth patch 𝒫⋐𝒮k​ℓ​(ϕ)\mathcal{P}\Subset\mathcal{S}_{k\ell}(\phi) away from multiway junctions, the differential of the router defines a finite-dimensional subspace 𝒱k​ℓ​(ϕ,𝒫)⊂Cc∞​(𝒫)\mathcal{V}_{k\ell}(\phi,\mathcal{P})\subset C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{P}) of realizable normal velocities. More precisely, every parameter direction vv induces a first-order normal velocity Vk​ℓ​[v]⋅nk​ℓ∈𝒱k​ℓ​(ϕ,𝒫)V_{k\ell}[v]\cdot n_{k\ell}\in\mathcal{V}_{k\ell}(\phi,\mathcal{P}), and conversely every φ∈𝒱k​ℓ​(ϕ,𝒫)\varphi\in\mathcal{V}_{k\ell}(\phi,\mathcal{P}) is produced by at least one such parameter direction.

Assumption 5.12 is a finite-dimensional realizability condition. We do not ask the router to produce every smooth boundary motion. We only ask that the nondegeneracy argument be carried out inside the family of interface velocities that the parameterization can actually see. For linear logits, for instance, the induced normal velocities on a fixed smooth patch are finite-dimensional affine functions of the ambient features, not arbitrary elements of Cc∞​(𝒫)C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{P}).

Before stating the theorem, it helps to keep the logic straight. The boundary-mass estimates and the teacher-router assumption give the reference configuration against which global minimizers are compared. The probabilistic specialization-gap condition prevents a wrong expert from imitating the correct one on too much of a teacher cell. The router realizability condition says which first-order interface motions are actually visible to the parameterization. The conditional part comes next, through the final two assumptions that transfer first- and second-order information from the hard problem to the soft one and impose the needed negative-curvature geometry on the profiled hard objective away from the teacher partition. Read in that order, the theorem is a reduction statement. It is not a blanket description of all MoE landscapes.

Assumption 5.13 (Soft-to-hard C1/C2C^{1}/C^{2} control near critical points).

Fix ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2). There exist τ0>0\tau_{0}>0 and a function r⁡(τ)↓0r(\tau)\downarrow 0 as τ↓0\tau\downarrow 0 such that for all τ∈(0,τ0]\tau\in(0,\tau_{0}] and all (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) in a neighborhood of any critical point under consideration,

‖∇ϕLτ​(θ,ϕ)−∇ϕL~0​(θ,ϕ)‖+|∇θLτ​(θ,ϕ)−∇θL~0​(θ,ϕ)|≤r⁡(τ),\|\nabla_{\phi}L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-\nabla_{\phi}\widetilde{L}_{0}(\theta,\phi)\|+\|\nabla_{\theta}L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)-\nabla_{\theta}\widetilde{L}_{0}(\theta,\phi)\|\leq r(\tau),

and the Hessian blocks satisfy

‖∇ϕ​ϕ2Lτ−∇ϕ​ϕ2L~0‖op+‖∇θ​ϕ2Lτ−∇θ​ϕ2L~0‖op+‖∇θ​θ2Lτ−∇θ​θ2L~0‖op≤r⁡(τ).\|\nabla^{2}_{\phi\phi}L_{\tau}-\nabla^{2}_{\phi\phi}\widetilde{L}_{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\nabla^{2}_{\theta\phi}L_{\tau}-\nabla^{2}_{\theta\phi}\widetilde{L}_{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\nabla^{2}_{\theta\theta}L_{\tau}-\nabla^{2}_{\theta\theta}\widetilde{L}_{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq r(\tau).

Assumption 5.13 replaces the earlier Hessian-only hypothesis. The strict-saddle step needs gradient transfer as well, because soft criticality must imply approximate hard criticality before one can invoke the shape calculus.

Assumption 5.14 (Frozen-partition expert geometry and realized interface nondegeneracy).

There exists αfr>0\alpha_{\mathrm{fr}}>0 such that for every router parameter ϕ\phi in the region under consideration, the hard-routing risk θ↦L~0​(θ,ϕ)\theta\mapsto\widetilde{L}_{0}(\theta,\phi) has a unique critical point θ^​(ϕ)\hat{\theta}(\phi), this critical point is the global minimizer in the expert variables, and

∇θ​θ2L~0​(θ^​(ϕ),ϕ)⪰αfr​I.\nabla^{2}_{\theta\theta}\widetilde{L}_{0}(\hat{\theta}(\phi),\phi)\succeq\alpha_{\mathrm{fr}}I.

Moreover, whenever the induced hard partition at ϕ\phi is not teacher-equivalent up to permutation, there exist an adjacent pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell), a smooth patch 𝒫⋐𝒮k​ℓ​(ϕ)\mathcal{P}\Subset\mathcal{S}_{k\ell}(\phi) away from multiway junctions, and a realized velocity φ∈𝒱k​ℓ​(ϕ,𝒫)∖{0}\varphi\in\mathcal{V}_{k\ell}(\phi,\mathcal{P})\setminus\{0\} such that the first variation of the profiled hard objective

Ψ0​(ϕ):=L~0​(θ^​(ϕ),ϕ)\Psi_{0}(\phi):=\widetilde{L}_{0}(\hat{\theta}(\phi),\phi)

vanishes along φ\varphi and the second variation satisfies

δ2​Ψ0​(ϕ)​[φ,φ]≤−λnd​‖φ‖L2​(𝒫,pX​d​ℋd−1)2\delta^{2}\Psi_{0}(\phi)[\varphi,\varphi]\leq-\lambda_{\mathrm{nd}}\|\varphi\|_{L^{2}(\mathcal{P},p_{X}d\mathcal{H}^{d-1})}^{2}

for some constant λnd>0\lambda_{\mathrm{nd}}>0 independent of the critical point.

Lemma 5.15 (Negative curvature persists under small C2C^{2} perturbations).

Let H0H_{0} and HH be symmetric matrices (or bounded self-adjoint operators) with ‖H−H0‖op≤η\|H-H_{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\eta. Then λmin​(H)≤λmin​(H0)+η\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq\lambda_{\min}(H_{0})+\eta. In particular, if λmin​(H0)≤−λ\lambda_{\min}(H_{0})\leq-\lambda and η≤λ/2\eta\leq\lambda/2, then λmin(H)≤−λ/2\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq-\lambda/2.

This is a standard consequence of the variational characterization λmin​(H)=inf‖u‖=1u⊤​H​u\lambda_{\min}(H)=\inf_{\|u\|=1}u^{\top}Hu and the inequality |u⊤​(H−H0)​u|≤‖H−H0‖op|u^{\top}(H-H_{0})u|\leq\|H-H_{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}. ∎

The next theorem is the main conditional optimization statement of the paper. For a router parameter ϕ\phi, we denote its hard cells by

Ωk​(ϕ):={x∈𝒳:k=k⋆​(x,ϕ)},\Omega_{k}(\phi):=\{x\in\mathcal{X}:\ k=k^{\star}(x;\phi)\}, (5.7)

where k⋆​(x,ϕ)k^{\star}(x;\phi) is the unique maximizing index outside the tie set and ties are assigned by a fixed deterministic rule on the remaining null set. For a candidate relabeling π\pi and parameters (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi), define the confidently misrouted interior set

ℰmis(π;θ,ϕ,τ):={x∈𝒳:x∈Ωk⋆,pj(τ)(x;ϕ)≥1−ε for some j≠π(k)}∩𝒢ε(τ;ϕ).\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau):=\Bigl\{x\in\mathcal{X}:\ x\in\Omega_{k}^{\star},p_{j}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\geq 1-\varepsilon\text{ for some }j\neq\pi(k)\Bigr\}\cap\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi). (5.8)

When (θ,ϕ,τ)(\theta,\phi,\tau) are fixed, we write this set simply as ℰmis​(π)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi).

Lemma 5.16 (Misrouting mass).

Assume Assumption 5.1, the uniform-boundedness branch of Assumption 5.2, and Assumption 5.11. Fix ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2) such that 2​ε​Bstu≤12​γgap2\varepsilon B_{\mathrm{stu}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}}. Then the following bound holds for every parameter pair (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi), every temperature τ>0\tau>0, and every permutation π\pi:

L~τ,int​(θ,ϕ)≥γgap4​max⁡{PX​(ℰmis​(π,θ,ϕ,τ))−K⁡(K−1)​ηgap,0}.\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{int}}(\theta,\phi)\geq\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}}{4}\,\max\{P_{X}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau))-K(K-1)\eta_{\mathrm{gap}},0\}. (5.9)

Consequently, if L~τ​(θ,ϕ)≤M\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)\leq M, then

PX​(ℰmis​(π,θ,ϕ,τ))≤4​Mγgap+K⁡(K−1)​ηgap.P_{X}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau))\leq\frac{4M}{\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}}+K(K-1)\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}. (5.10)

Fix π\pi. On ℰmis​(π,θ,ϕ,τ)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau), the point belongs to some teacher cell Ωk⋆\Omega_{k}^{\star} and the soft router assigns weight at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon to a student expert j≠π⁡(k)j\neq\pi(k). The bounded-expert hypothesis gives

|hθ,ϕ,τ​(x)−fj​(x,θj)|≤∑m≠jpm(τ)​(x,ϕ)​|fm​(x,θm)−fj​(x,θj)|≤2​ε​Bstu.\left\lvert h_{\theta,\phi,\tau}(x)-f_{j}(x;\theta_{j})\right\rvert\leq\sum_{m\neq j}p_{m}^{(\tau)}(x;\phi)\left\lvert f_{m}(x;\theta_{m})-f_{j}(x;\theta_{j})\right\rvert\leq 2\varepsilon B_{\mathrm{stu}}. (5.11)

Ek​j:={x∈Ωk⋆:(fj​(x,θj)−fk⋆​(x))2≤γgap},Egap​(π):=⋃k=1K⋃j≠π⁡(k)Ek​j.E_{kj}:=\Bigl\{x\in\Omega_{k}^{\star}:(f_{j}(x;\theta_{j})-f_{k}^{\star}(x))^{2}\leq\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}\Bigr\},\qquad E_{\mathrm{gap}}(\pi):=\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\bigcup_{j\neq\pi(k)}E_{kj}. (5.12)

If x∈ℰmis​(π,θ,ϕ,τ)∖Egap​(π)x\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau)\setminus E_{\mathrm{gap}}(\pi), then the dominating expert is at least γgap\sqrt{\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}} away from the teacher signal on that cell before the soft-mixture error in (5.11). Since 2​ε​Bstu≤12​γgap2\varepsilon B_{\mathrm{stu}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}}, the squared residual is at least γgap/4\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}/4 on this set. The next theorem is the main conditional optimization statement of the paper. The global-minimizer part is a consequence of the preceding comparison estimates and the matching lemma, while the strict-saddle part depends on the profiled hard-routing geometry and the soft-to-hard derivative transfer encoded above.

Theorem 5.17 (Conditional landscape-transfer principle).

Suppose all assumptions stated above in this section hold, and assume the uniform-boundedness branch of Assumption 5.2. Fix ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2) so that

2​ε​Bstu≤12​γgap.2\varepsilon B_{\mathrm{stu}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\gamma_{\mathrm{gap}}}.

Then there exists τ0>0\tau_{0}>0 such that the following conclusions hold for every τ∈(0,τ0]\tau\in(0,\tau_{0}]. For any global minimizer (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) of LτL_{\tau}, there is a permutation π\pi of {1,…,K}\{1,\dots,K\} such that

∑k=1K𝔼⁡[|fπ⁡(k)​(X,θπ⁡(k))−fk⋆​(X)|2​ 1Ωk⋆​(X)]≤C1​(BMϕ⋆​(τ,ε)+BMϕ​(τ,ε)+ηgap+ε2),\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\left\lvert f_{\pi(k)}(X;\theta_{\pi(k)})-f_{k}^{\star}(X)\right\rvert^{2}\,\mathds{1}_{\Omega_{k}^{\star}}(X)\bigr]\leq C_{1}\,\Bigl(\mathrm{BM}_{\phi^{\star}}(\tau;\varepsilon)+\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon)+\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}+\varepsilon^{2}\Bigr), (5.13)

and the induced partition (Ωk​(ϕ))(\Omega_{k}(\phi)) satisfies

∑k=1Kℙ⁡((Ωπ⁡(k)​(ϕ)​△​Ωk⋆)∩𝒢ε​(τ,ϕ))≤C2​(BMϕ⋆​(τ,ε)+ηgap+ε2),\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{P}\bigl((\Omega_{\pi(k)}(\phi)\triangle\Omega_{k}^{\star})\cap\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\bigr)\leq C_{2}\,\bigl(\mathrm{BM}_{\phi^{\star}}(\tau;\varepsilon)+\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}+\varepsilon^{2}\bigr), (5.14)

where C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are independent of τ\tau for fixed ε\varepsilon and ηgap\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}. In addition, every critical point (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) of LτL_{\tau} whose induced hard partition is not teacher-equivalent up to permutation is a strict saddle, in the sense that the Hessian of LτL_{\tau} at (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) has at least one negative eigenvalue.

Proof.

All constants below are uniform for τ∈(0,τ0]\tau\in(0,\tau_{0}]. We first isolate the boundary-layer contribution and then compare the soft objective with the teacher configuration away from that layer. This yields the global-minimum statement. We then turn to the remaining critical points and show that the hard negative curvature persists for sufficiently small temperature.

We begin with the boundary contribution. By Lemma 5.5,

L~τ​(θ,ϕ)=L~τ,int​(θ,ϕ)+L~τ,bdry​(θ,ϕ),L~τ,bdry​(θ,ϕ)≤C​BMϕ​(τ,ε).\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)=\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{int}}(\theta,\phi)+\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{bdry}}(\theta,\phi),\qquad\widetilde{L}_{\tau,\mathrm{bdry}}(\theta,\phi)\leq C\,\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon).

Thus every place where the soft model can differ substantially from the hard-routing picture is already confined to a boundary layer of size O​(BMϕ​(τ,ε))O(\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon)).

The next point is to compare with the teacher configuration and quantify the cost of confident misrouting. At the teacher parameters (θ⋆,ϕ⋆)(\theta^{\star},\phi^{\star}), the hard predictor agrees with the teacher signal outside a PXP_{X}-null tie set, and the remaining soft-versus-hard discrepancy is controlled by the same boundary layer. Combining the softmax tail estimate with the teacher-router regularity, equivalently Corollary 4.4 applied to ϕ⋆\phi^{\star}, gives

L~τ​(θ⋆,ϕ⋆)≤C0​BMϕ⋆​(τ,ε)+C0​ε2.\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta^{\star},\phi^{\star})\leq C_{0}\,\mathrm{BM}_{\phi^{\star}}(\tau;\varepsilon)+C_{0}\varepsilon^{2}. (5.15)

After decreasing ε\varepsilon once and for all, the harmless ε2\varepsilon^{2} term is absorbed into the constants in the final estimates.

These estimates force global minimizers to stay close to the teacher after a matching of student experts to teacher cells. Let (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) be a global minimizer and choose a permutation π\pi that minimizes PX​(ℰmis​(π,θ,ϕ,τ))P_{X}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau)) among all relabelings. Since global minimality gives L~τ​(θ,ϕ)≤L~τ​(θ⋆,ϕ⋆)\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)\leq\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta^{\star},\phi^{\star}), Lemma 5.16 and (5.15) imply

PX​(ℰmis​(π,θ,ϕ,τ))≲BMϕ⋆​(τ,ε)+ηgap+ε2.P_{X}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau))\lesssim\mathrm{BM}_{\phi^{\star}}(\tau;\varepsilon)+\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}+\varepsilon^{2}. (5.16)

In this form the matching step is explicit. A one-to-one relabeling is chosen first, and the specialization gap then rules out large confidently misrouted interior mass under that relabeling, except on the allowed exceptional sets and the boundary layer.

On the good interior region

Ak:=Ωk⋆∩𝒢ε(τ;ϕ)∩ℰmis(π;θ,ϕ,τ)c∩{pπ⁡(k)(τ)(X;ϕ)≥1−ε},A_{k}:=\Omega_{k}^{\star}\cap\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\cap\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau)^{c}\cap\{p_{\pi(k)}^{(\tau)}(X;\phi)\geq 1-\varepsilon\}, (5.17)

the router gives expert π⁡(k)\pi(k) weight at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon. Applying Proposition 5.8 after relabeling the student experts by π\pi and summing over kk gives

∑k=1K𝔼⁡[|fπ⁡(k)​(X,θπ⁡(k))−fk⋆​(X)|2​ 1Ak​(X)]≲L~τ​(θ,ϕ)+ε2.\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\left\lvert f_{\pi(k)}(X;\theta_{\pi(k)})-f_{k}^{\star}(X)\right\rvert^{2}\,\mathds{1}_{A_{k}}(X)\Bigr]\lesssim\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)+\varepsilon^{2}.

L~τ​(θ,ϕ)≤L~τ​(θ⋆,ϕ⋆)≲BMϕ⋆​(τ,ε)+ε2\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)\leq\widetilde{L}_{\tau}(\theta^{\star},\phi^{\star})\lesssim\mathrm{BM}_{\phi^{\star}}(\tau;\varepsilon)+\varepsilon^{2}

by (5.15). Moreover,

Ωk⋆∖Ak⊆𝒰ε​(τ,ϕ)∪ℰmis​(π,θ,ϕ,τ).\Omega_{k}^{\star}\setminus A_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\cup\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau).

Summing over kk and using (5.16) yields

∑k=1K𝔼⁡[|fπ⁡(k)​(X,θπ⁡(k))−fk⋆​(X)|2​ 1Ωk⋆​(X)]≲BMϕ⋆​(τ,ε)+BMϕ​(τ,ε)+ηgap+ε2,\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\left\lvert f_{\pi(k)}(X;\theta_{\pi(k)})-f_{k}^{\star}(X)\right\rvert^{2}\,\mathds{1}_{\Omega_{k}^{\star}}(X)\bigr]\lesssim\mathrm{BM}_{\phi^{\star}}(\tau;\varepsilon)+\mathrm{BM}_{\phi}(\tau;\varepsilon)+\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}+\varepsilon^{2},

For the partition estimate, fix x∈𝒢ε​(τ,ϕ)x\in\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi). If x∈Ωk⋆x\in\Omega_{k}^{\star} and the induced hard cell after relabeling is not Ωπ⁡(k)​(ϕ)\Omega_{\pi(k)}(\phi), then the expert receiving weight at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon is wrong relative to the selected matching. ⋃k=1K((Ωπ⁡(k)​(ϕ)​△​Ωk⋆)∩𝒢ε​(τ,ϕ))⊆ℰmis​(π,θ,ϕ,τ),\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\bigl((\Omega_{\pi(k)}(\phi)\triangle\Omega_{k}^{\star})\cap\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\bigr)\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau),

and hence, after absorbing the combinatorial counting factor into the constant,

∑k=1Kℙ⁡((Ωπ⁡(k)​(ϕ)​△​Ωk⋆)∩𝒢ε​(τ,ϕ))≲PX​(ℰmis​(π,θ,ϕ,τ))≲BMϕ⋆​(τ,ε)+ηgap+ε2,\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{P}\bigl((\Omega_{\pi(k)}(\phi)\triangle\Omega_{k}^{\star})\cap\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\tau;\phi)\bigr)\lesssim P_{X}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{mis}}(\pi;\theta,\phi,\tau))\lesssim\mathrm{BM}_{\phi^{\star}}(\tau;\varepsilon)+\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}+\varepsilon^{2},

which is (5.14) after absorbing the fixed ε2\varepsilon^{2} term into the constant for the chosen tolerance.

It remains to analyze critical points whose induced hard partition is not teacher-equivalent up to permutation. Let (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) be such a critical point of LτL_{\tau}. Since ∇Lτ​(θ,ϕ)=0\nabla L_{\tau}(\theta,\phi)=0 and Assumption 5.13 gives gradient control, the hard objective is approximately critical at the same point:

‖∇θL~0​(θ,ϕ)‖+‖∇ϕL~0​(θ,ϕ)‖≤r⁡(τ).\|\nabla_{\theta}\widetilde{L}_{0}(\theta,\phi)\|+\|\nabla_{\phi}\widetilde{L}_{0}(\theta,\phi)\|\leq r(\tau).

For the frozen partition induced by ϕ\phi, Assumption 5.14 gives a unique expert minimizer θ^​(ϕ)\hat{\theta}(\phi) and a uniformly positive θ​θ\theta\theta Hessian. The usual strong-convexity estimate in the expert block then gives

‖θ−θ^​(ϕ)‖≲r⁡(τ).\|\theta-\hat{\theta}(\phi)\|\lesssim r(\tau).

Consequently the Morse index near (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) is determined, up to an O⁡(r⁡(τ))O(r(\tau)) perturbation, by the Schur complement associated with the profiled hard objective

Ψ0​(ϕ):=L~0​(θ^​(ϕ),ϕ).\Psi_{0}(\phi):=\widetilde{L}_{0}(\hat{\theta}(\phi),\phi).

Since the point under consideration has a non-teacher-equivalent hard partition, Assumption 5.14 supplies an adjacent pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell), a smooth patch 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and a realized velocity φ∈𝒱k​ℓ​(ϕ,𝒫)\varphi\in\mathcal{V}_{k\ell}(\phi,\mathcal{P}) for which the first variation of Ψ0\Psi_{0} vanishes and

δ2​Ψ0​(ϕ)​[φ,φ]≤−λnd​‖φ‖L2​(𝒫,pX​d​ℋd−1)2.\delta^{2}\Psi_{0}(\phi)[\varphi,\varphi]\leq-\lambda_{\mathrm{nd}}\|\varphi\|_{L^{2}(\mathcal{P},p_{X}d\mathcal{H}^{d-1})}^{2}.

By Assumption 5.12, choose a router parameter direction vv realizing this velocity. Proposition 5.10 identifies the first variation along such localized interface motions; the second variation bound is part of the profiled hard-geometry hypothesis. Therefore the profiled hard Hessian has a negative quadratic form along vv after rescaling inside the finite-dimensional realized-velocity space.

Assumption 5.13 now transfers this negative curvature from the hard profiled problem to the soft objective: the Hessian blocks of LτL_{\tau} differ from those of L~0\widetilde{L}_{0} by at most r⁡(τ)r(\tau) in operator norm, so the corresponding Schur complement and hence the full Hessian differ by O⁡(r⁡(τ))O(r(\tau)) on the finite-dimensional local chart. Lemma 5.15 preserves a negative eigenvalue once r⁡(τ)r(\tau) is smaller than a fixed fraction of λnd\lambda_{\mathrm{nd}}. Thus the Hessian of LτL_{\tau} has a negative eigenvalue at (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi), and the critical point is a strict saddle.

This proves the theorem. ∎

Remark 5.18 (Landscape and optimization).

Theorem 5.17 is a population statement, and its conditional nature should stay visible. The strict-saddle conclusion depends on two inputs that are not proved here: the curvature hypothesis for the profiled hard-routing problem and the derivative transfer from soft to hard routing. Once those are granted, the conclusion is that critical points with non-teacher-equivalent hard partitions have a negative-curvature direction for sufficiently small τ\tau. From an optimization point of view this is consistent with the usual picture in which gradient methods started from generic points either approach the minimizing set or escape through negative curvature, especially when the updates carry some noise; see, for example, [4, 10]. A fully rigorous SGD statement would require a separate dynamical analysis, which is beyond the scope of the present paper.

6 A reduced Gaussian calculation for symmetry breaking

The previous section gives a conditional description of the small-temperature population landscape, but it does not attempt to model the full training dynamics by which specialization first appears. The section is narrower. It gives a reduced two-expert Gaussian calculation that isolates one local instability by which a nearly balanced router, coupled to a small expert contrast, is driven toward alignment with the teacher separator. The calculation is meant as a mechanism check for the interface viewpoint, not as a global convergence theorem for coupled MoE training.

6.1 Setup

Let X∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with positive-definite covariance matrix Σ\Sigma. Let v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖v‖=1\left\lVert v\right\rVert=1 and define the teacher partition

Ω1⋆:={x:⟨v,x⟩≥0},Ω2⋆:={x:⟨v,x⟩<0}.\Omega_{1}^{\star}:=\{x:\left\langle v,\,x\right\rangle\geq 0\},\qquad\Omega_{2}^{\star}:=\{x:\left\langle v,\,x\right\rangle<0\}.

The teacher consists of two linear experts with shared baseline m:𝒳→ℝm:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}, where here 𝒳=ℝd\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{d}.

f1⋆​(x):=m⁡(x)+12​d∗⊤​x,f2⋆​(x):=m⁡(x)−12​d∗⊤​x,f_{1}^{\star}(x):=m(x)+\tfrac{1}{2}d_{*}^{\top}x,\qquad f_{2}^{\star}(x):=m(x)-\tfrac{1}{2}d_{*}^{\top}x,

for some fixed contrast vector d∗∈ℝdd_{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. On each side of the separator the expert means differ by d∗⊤​xd_{*}^{\top}x, so the teacher contrast is linear with direction d∗d_{*}. For clarity, we consider a noiseless teacher.

Y=f1⋆​(X)​𝟙X∈Ω1⋆+f2⋆​(X)​𝟙X∈Ω2⋆.Y=f_{1}^{\star}(X)\mathds{1}_{X\in\Omega_{1}^{\star}}+f_{2}^{\star}(X)\mathds{1}_{X\in\Omega_{2}^{\star}}.

The case with additive bounded noise can be handled with minor modifications and does not change the symmetry-breaking conclusions (it adds only bounded perturbations to the moment expressions below and does not change their signs under the same non-degeneracy assumptions).

The student is a two-expert MoE with linear experts

f1​(x,θ1)=a⊤​x+b,f2​(x,θ2)=c⊤​x+d,f_{1}(x;\theta_{1})=a^{\top}x+b,\qquad f_{2}(x;\theta_{2})=c^{\top}x+d,

and a router that uses antisymmetric scores

a1​(x,u)=u⊤​x,a2​(x,u)=−u⊤​x,a_{1}(x;u)=u^{\top}x,\qquad a_{2}(x;u)=-u^{\top}x,

for a router parameter u∈ℝdu\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The corresponding softmax weights are

p1(τ)​(x,u)=σ⁡(2​u⊤​xτ),p2(τ)​(x,u)=1−p1(τ)​(x,u),p_{1}^{(\tau)}(x;u)=\sigma\Bigl(\frac{2u^{\top}x}{\tau}\Bigr),\qquad p_{2}^{(\tau)}(x;u)=1-p_{1}^{(\tau)}(x;u),

where σ⁡(z)=1/(1+e−z)\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z}) and τ>0\tau>0 is the router temperature. The student prediction is

hθ,u,τ​(x):=p1(τ)​(x,u)​f1​(x,θ1)+p2(τ)​(x,u)​f2​(x,θ2).h_{\theta,u,\tau}(x):=p_{1}^{(\tau)}(x;u)f_{1}(x;\theta_{1})+p_{2}^{(\tau)}(x;u)f_{2}(x;\theta_{2}).

For fixed temperature in this subsection, we use the shorthand h⁡(X,u,θ):=hθ,u,τ​(X)h(X;u,\theta):=h_{\theta,u,\tau}(X).

We consider gradient descent on the squared risk

Lτ​(u,θ):=𝔼⁡[(Y−h⁡(X,u,θ))2],L_{\tau}(u,\theta):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(Y-h(X;u,\theta))^{2}\bigr],

starting from a symmetric initialization where

u≈0,(a,b)≈(c,d),u\approx 0,\qquad(a,b)\approx(c,d),

so that initially the two experts are nearly identical and the router is nearly balanced. At exact symmetry, f1=f2f_{1}=f_{2} and h⁡(⋅,u,θ)h(\cdot;u,\theta) is independent of uu, reflecting the permutation symmetry between experts. In practice, small random perturbations in the expert parameters or stochastic gradients break this perfect symmetry and induce a small but non-zero expert contrast. The question is then whether the router amplifies this contrast and aligns with the teacher separator vv, or whether the symmetric state remains stable.

6.2 Linearization and effective operator

This subsection does not try to derive the full coupled gradient-flow system for router and experts. That would obscure the mechanism we actually want to see. Instead we isolate a reduced model for the onset of symmetry breaking, in the regime where the experts have already developed a small contrast while the router is still near balance. Concretely, we linearize the router dynamics around u=0u=0, treat the expert contrast as slowly varying input, and read off the effective operator that decides whether the symmetric router is stable.

For fixed expert parameters θ:=(θ1,θ2)\theta:=(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}), the gradient of the risk with respect to uu is

∇uLτ​(u,θ)=−2​𝔼​[(Y−h⁡(X,u,θ))​∂uh⁡(X,u,θ)].\nabla_{u}L_{\tau}(u,\theta)=-2\,\mathbb{E}\Bigl[(Y-h(X;u,\theta))\,\partial_{u}h(X;u,\theta)\Bigr]. (6.1)

Since

hθ,u,τ​(x)=p1(τ)​(x,u)​f1​(x,θ1)+p2(τ)​(x,u)​f2​(x,θ2),h_{\theta,u,\tau}(x)=p_{1}^{(\tau)}(x;u)\,f_{1}(x;\theta_{1})+p_{2}^{(\tau)}(x;u)\,f_{2}(x;\theta_{2}),

and

∂up1(τ)(x;u)=2τp1(τ)(x;u)p2(τ)(x;u)x,∂up2(τ)(x;u)=−∂up1(τ)(x;u),\partial_{u}p_{1}^{(\tau)}(x;u)=\frac{2}{\tau}\,p_{1}^{(\tau)}(x;u)p_{2}^{(\tau)}(x;u)\,x,\qquad\partial_{u}p_{2}^{(\tau)}(x;u)=-\partial_{u}p_{1}^{(\tau)}(x;u),

we obtain

∂uhθ,u,τ​(x)=2τ​p1(τ)​(x,u)​p2(τ)​(x,u)​(f1​(x,θ1)−f2​(x,θ2))​x.\partial_{u}h_{\theta,u,\tau}(x)=\frac{2}{\tau}\,p_{1}^{(\tau)}(x;u)p_{2}^{(\tau)}(x;u)\,\bigl(f_{1}(x;\theta_{1})-f_{2}(x;\theta_{2})\bigr)\,x.

Substituting into (6.1) gives

∇uLτ​(u,θ)=−4τ​𝔼​[(Y−h⁡(X,u,θ))​p1(τ)​(X,u)​p2(τ)​(X,u)​(f1​(X,θ1)−f2​(X,θ2))​X].\nabla_{u}L_{\tau}(u,\theta)=-\frac{4}{\tau}\,\mathbb{E}\Bigl[(Y-h(X;u,\theta))\,p_{1}^{(\tau)}(X;u)p_{2}^{(\tau)}(X;u)\,\bigl(f_{1}(X;\theta_{1})-f_{2}(X;\theta_{2})\bigr)\,X\Bigr]. (6.2)

Near a symmetric configuration where uu is small and the experts have already started to align with the teacher, the expression simplifies in two complementary ways. First, for fixed τ\tau and small uu, the factor p1​p2p_{1}p_{2} is approximately 1/41/4; more precisely, its Taylor expansion has the form p1(τ)​p2(τ)=1/4+O⁡((u⊤​X)2/τ2)p_{1}^{(\tau)}p_{2}^{(\tau)}=1/4+O((u^{\top}X)^{2}/\tau^{2}) on bounded score regions. Thus the radius of this linearization shrinks with τ\tau, and the reduced calculation should be read locally in uu for the chosen temperature. Second, the signed product (Y−h)​(f1−f2)(Y-h)\bigl(f_{1}-f_{2}\bigr) is precisely the quantity that records whether the current expert contrast is being reinforced by the residual. In symmetry-breaking regimes this product correlates with the teacher side through v⊤​Xv^{\top}X and changes sign when that teacher side is flipped.

A genuine linearization in uu must produce a term of the form M​uMu, not a uu-independent drift. This requires the signed product (Y−h)​(f1−f2)(Y-h)(f_{1}-f_{2}) to depend to first order on the router score u⊤​Xu^{\top}X in an odd way. Rather than deriving that dependence from the full coupled training dynamics, we isolate it as an explicit response assumption. For uu near the origin, assume there exists a measurable function ψ:ℝ×ℝ→ℝ\psi:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, depending on the router score s:=u⊤​Xs:=u^{\top}X and teacher score t:=v⊤​Xt:=v^{\top}X, such that:

(Y−h⁡(X,u,θ))​(f1​(X,θ1)−f2​(X,θ2))=ψ⁡(u⊤​X,v⊤​X)​(d∗⊤​X)+ru​(X),(Y-h(X;u,\theta))\bigl(f_{1}(X;\theta_{1})-f_{2}(X;\theta_{2})\bigr)=\psi(u^{\top}X,v^{\top}X)\,(d_{*}^{\top}X)+r_{u}(X), (6.3)

where ψ⁡(⋅,t)\psi(\cdot,t) is odd in its first argument for each fixed tt, is differentiable at s=0s=0, and has derivative ∂sψ⁡(0,t)=:g⁡(t)\partial_{s}\psi(0,t)=:g(t) for a measurable scalar function gg. We assume moreover that gg is odd and satisfies g⁡(z)​z≥0g(z)z\geq 0 for all zz, so the feedback is aligned with the teacher side rather than opposed to it, and that the remainder obeys 𝔼⁡[|ru​(X)|​‖X‖]=o⁡(‖u‖)\mathbb{E}[|r_{u}(X)|\,\|X\|]=o(\|u\|) as u→0u\to 0. This assumption should be read as a reduced linearized model for the early symmetry-breaking regime, not as a theorem about the full coupled MoE dynamics. In plain terms, it says the residual–contrast product reacts linearly to a small router imbalance, the sign of that reaction is tied to the teacher side v⊤​Xv^{\top}X, and the resulting feedback reinforces rather than cancels the existing expert contrast.

Under (6.3), the linearization is straightforward. For fixed temperature, the softmax factor satisfies p1(τ)​p2(τ)=1/4+O⁡((u⊤​X)2/τ2)p_{1}^{(\tau)}p_{2}^{(\tau)}=1/4+O((u^{\top}X)^{2}/\tau^{2}) near u=0u=0 on bounded score regions, while the response term satisfies ψ⁡(u⊤​X,v⊤​X)=(u⊤​X)​g​(v⊤​X)+o⁡(‖u‖​‖X‖)\psi(u^{\top}X,v^{\top}X)=(u^{\top}X)g(v^{\top}X)+o(\|u\|\|X\|). Substituting these expansions into (6.2) and using the remainder condition on rur_{u} gives

∇uLτ​(u,θ)=−1τ​𝔼​[(u⊤​X)​g​(v⊤​X)​(d∗⊤​X)​X]+o⁡(‖u‖)=−1τ​M​u+o⁡(‖u‖),\nabla_{u}L_{\tau}(u,\theta)=-\frac{1}{\tau}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[(u^{\top}X)\,g(v^{\top}X)\,(d_{*}^{\top}X)\,X\bigr]+o(\left\lVert u\right\rVert)=-\frac{1}{\tau}\,Mu+o(\left\lVert u\right\rVert), (6.4)

where the effective linear operator MM is the symmetric matrix

M:=𝔼⁡[g⁡(v⊤​X)​(d∗⊤​X)​X​X⊤].M:=\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(v^{\top}X)\,(d_{*}^{\top}X)\,XX^{\top}\bigr]. (6.5)

(The matrix is symmetric because it is an expectation of a scalar times X​X⊤XX^{\top}.)

Under (6.4), a gradient descent step with learning rate η>0\eta>0 yields the linearized dynamics

ut+1=ut−η​∇uLτ​(ut,θ)=(I+ητ​M)​ut+o⁡(‖ut‖).u_{t+1}=u_{t}-\eta\nabla_{u}L_{\tau}(u_{t},\theta)=\Bigl(I+\frac{\eta}{\tau}M\Bigr)u_{t}+o(\|u_{t}\|). (6.6)

The spectrum of MM controls whether the symmetric state u≈0u\approx 0 is stable or unstable. Directions corresponding to positive eigenvalues of MM grow under gradient descent, while those with negative eigenvalues decay.

6.3 Gaussian moments along the teacher separator

We now compute the action of MM along the teacher separator vv in the Gaussian case. We begin with a general expression that applies to any odd response function gg that depends on XX only through v⊤​Xv^{\top}X, and then specialize to concrete choices.

Lemma 6.1 (Gaussian moment along vv for general response).

Let X∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma), ‖v‖=1\left\lVert v\right\rVert=1, and suppose the response function has the form g⁡(v⊤​X)g(v^{\top}X) where g:ℝ→ℝg:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is measurable, odd, and satisfies g⁡(z)​z≥0g(z)z\geq 0 for all zz and 𝔼⁡[|g⁡(v⊤​X)|​|v⊤​X|3]<∞\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert g(v^{\top}X)\right\rvert\left\lvert v^{\top}X\right\rvert^{3}]<\infty. Let MM be given by (6.5). Then

v⊤​M​v=κg​(d∗⊤​Σ​v)​v⊤​Σ​v,v^{\top}Mv=\kappa_{g}\,(d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v)\,\sqrt{v^{\top}\Sigma v},

where for s2:=v⊤​Σ​vs^{2}:=v^{\top}\Sigma v and G∼𝒩⁡(0,s2)G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,s^{2}),

κg:=𝔼⁡[g⁡(G)​G3]s3.\kappa_{g}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}[g(G)G^{3}]}{s^{3}}.

In particular, if gg is not identically zero and satisfies g⁡(z)≥0g(z)\geq 0 for z≥0z\geq 0, then κg>0\kappa_{g}>0 and

sign⁡(v⊤​M​v)=sign⁡(d∗⊤​Σ​v).\mathrm{sign}\bigl(v^{\top}Mv\bigr)=\mathrm{sign}\bigl(d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v\bigr).
Proof.

Let Z:=v⊤​X∼𝒩⁡(0,s2)Z:=v^{\top}X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,s^{2}) with s2:=v⊤​Σ​vs^{2}:=v^{\top}\Sigma v. By Gaussian regression,

𝔼[X∣Z=z]=Σ​vv⊤​Σ​vz=:αz,Cov(X∣Z)=Σ−Σ​v​v⊤​Σv⊤​Σ​v=:Σ⟂,\mathbb{E}[X\mid Z=z]=\frac{\Sigma v}{v^{\top}\Sigma v}\,z=:\alpha z,\qquad\Cov(X\mid Z)=\Sigma-\frac{\Sigma vv^{\top}\Sigma}{v^{\top}\Sigma v}=:\Sigma_{\perp},

and we can write X=α​Z+εX=\alpha Z+\varepsilon with ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ⟂)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{\perp}) independent of ZZ.

We compute

v⊤​M​v=𝔼⁡[g⁡(Z)​(d∗⊤​X)​(v⊤​X)2]=𝔼⁡[g⁡(Z)​(d∗⊤​X)​Z2].v^{\top}Mv=\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(Z)\,(d_{*}^{\top}X)\,(v^{\top}X)^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(Z)\,(d_{*}^{\top}X)\,Z^{2}\bigr].

Conditioning on ZZ and using 𝔼⁡[ε∣Z]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid Z]=0 gives

𝔼⁡[d∗⊤​X∣Z=z]=d∗⊤​(α​z)=(d∗⊤​Σ​v)​zs2.\mathbb{E}[d_{*}^{\top}X\mid Z=z]=d_{*}^{\top}(\alpha z)=(d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v)\,\frac{z}{s^{2}}.

Hence

v⊤​M​v=(d∗⊤​Σ​v)​1s2​𝔼​[g⁡(Z)​Z3].v^{\top}Mv=(d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v)\,\frac{1}{s^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}[g(Z)Z^{3}].

Writing ZZ as G∼𝒩⁡(0,s2)G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,s^{2}) yields

v⊤​M​v=(d∗⊤​Σ​v)​1s2​𝔼​[g⁡(G)​G3]=κg​(d∗⊤​Σ​v)​s,v^{\top}Mv=(d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v)\,\frac{1}{s^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}[g(G)G^{3}]=\kappa_{g}\,(d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v)\,s,

with κg:=𝔼⁡[g⁡(G)​G3]/s3\kappa_{g}:=\mathbb{E}[g(G)G^{3}]/s^{3} and s=v⊤​Σ​vs=\sqrt{v^{\top}\Sigma v}.

If gg is odd and g⁡(z)≥0g(z)\geq 0 for z≥0z\geq 0, then

𝔼[g(G)G3]=2∫0∞g(z)z312​π​se−z2/(2s2)dz>0,\mathbb{E}[g(G)G^{3}]=2\int_{0}^{\infty}g(z)z^{3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}s}e^{-z^{2}/(2s^{2})}\,\mathrm{d}z>0,

because the integrand is non-negative for all z≥0z\geq 0 and strictly positive on a set of positive measure (since gg is not identically zero). ∎

Two concrete choices of gg are particularly natural. One is the sign response g⁡(z)=sign⁡(z)g(z)=\mathrm{sign}(z), which corresponds to a router that reacts only to the side of the teacher hyperplane. The other is the smooth response g⁡(z)=tanh⁡(γ​z)g(z)=\tanh(\gamma z), with γ>0\gamma>0, which is more faithful to the softmax router. For the sign response we recover an explicit formula.

Lemma 6.2 (Alignment along vv for sign response).

Let X∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma), g⁡(z)=sign⁡(z)g(z)=\mathrm{sign}(z) with ‖v‖=1\left\lVert v\right\rVert=1, and MM as in (6.5). Then

v⊤​M​v=cG​(d∗⊤​Σ​v)​v⊤​Σ​v,cG=2​2π>0.v^{\top}Mv=c_{G}\,(d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v)\,\sqrt{v^{\top}\Sigma v},\qquad c_{G}=2\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}>0.

In particular, if d∗⊤​Σ​v≠0d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v\neq 0 then v⊤​M​v≠0v^{\top}Mv\neq 0.

Proof.

This is the special case of Lemma 6.1 with g⁡(z)=sign⁡(z)g(z)=\mathrm{sign}(z), so g⁡(G)​G3=|G|3g(G)G^{3}=\left\lvert G\right\rvert^{3} for G∼𝒩⁡(0,s2)G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,s^{2}). A standard Gaussian moment computation gives

𝔼⁡[|G|3]=2​2π​s3.\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert G\right\rvert^{3}]=2\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\,s^{3}.

Thus κg=2​2/π\kappa_{g}=2\sqrt{2/\pi} and the stated formula follows. ∎

For the smooth response g⁡(z)=tanh⁡(γ​z)g(z)=\tanh(\gamma z) one obtains a similar formula with a different positive constant κg=κ⁡(γ)>0\kappa_{g}=\kappa(\gamma)>0; the sign and qualitative behavior are the same.

6.4 Symmetry breaking and alignment

We now combine the linearization (6.6) with Lemma 6.1 to show that, whenever the teacher contrast d∗d_{*} has a non-zero projection along the separator vv, the symmetric router is linearly unstable in at least one direction correlated with vv.

A notational simplification is convenient before the theorem. Since the teacher partition is unchanged if we replace vv by −v-v and swap Ω1⋆,Ω2⋆\Omega_{1}^{\star},\Omega_{2}^{\star}, we may assume without loss of generality that

d∗⊤​Σ​v>0,d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v>0, (6.7)

whenever d∗⊤​Σ​v≠0d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v\neq 0.

The proposition below is local in scope. It does not claim a full dynamical description of training. Rather, it identifies the sign of the first instability at the symmetric router and shows that this instability necessarily has a component along the teacher separator.

Proposition 6.3 (Reduced linear instability of the symmetric router).

In the Gaussian two-expert setting above, assume the response expansion (6.3) holds with ∂sψ⁡(0,t)=g⁡(t)\partial_{s}\psi(0,t)=g(t) where gg is odd, g⁡(z)​z≥0g(z)z\geq 0, and not identically zero. Assume also d∗⊤​Σ​v≠0d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v\neq 0 (equivalently, after possibly flipping vv, (6.7) holds). Let MM be as in (6.5). Then the Rayleigh quotient has the following explicit form.

v⊤​M​v=κg​(d∗⊤​Σ​v)​v⊤​Σ​v,κg>0.v^{\top}Mv=\kappa_{g}\,(d_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v)\,\sqrt{v^{\top}\Sigma v},\qquad\kappa_{g}>0.

In particular v⊤​M​v>0v^{\top}Mv>0 under (6.7). Consequently, MM has at least one positive eigenvalue. Moreover, there is an eigenvector w+w_{+} with eigenvalue λ+>0\lambda_{+}>0 such that

⟨w+,v⟩≠0,\left\langle w_{+},\,v\right\rangle\neq 0,

so the unstable eigendirection has nontrivial correlation with the teacher separator. For gradient descent with step size η>0\eta>0, the linearized update ut+1≈(I+η​M/τ)​utu_{t+1}\approx(I+\eta M/\tau)u_{t} is unstable along w+w_{+} whenever 1+η​λ+/τ>11+\eta\lambda_{+}/\tau>1, equivalently whenever η​λ+/τ>0\eta\lambda_{+}/\tau>0. Thus, for fixed η>0\eta>0 and sufficiently small τ\tau, the symmetric point u=0u=0 is linearly unstable and the router parameter utu_{t} is driven toward a direction correlated with vv.

Proof.

The Rayleigh-quotient identity is exactly Lemma 6.1. Under the standing assumptions on gg, κg>0\kappa_{g}>0, so the sign of v⊤​M​vv^{\top}Mv is the sign of d∗⊤​Σ​vd_{*}^{\top}\Sigma v.

To obtain the spectral consequence, let {(wi,λi)}i=1d\{(w_{i},\lambda_{i})\}_{i=1}^{d} be an orthonormal eigen-decomposition. Then

v⊤​M​v=∑i=1dλi​⟨v,wi⟩2.v^{\top}Mv=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}\,\left\langle v,\,w_{i}\right\rangle^{2}.

If v⊤​M​v>0v^{\top}Mv>0, at least one summand must be strictly positive, so there exists an index ii with λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 and ⟨v,wi⟩≠0\left\langle v,\,w_{i}\right\rangle\neq 0. Taking w+:=wiw_{+}:=w_{i} and λ+:=λi\lambda_{+}:=\lambda_{i} proves the claim.

The instability statement then follows by writing the linearized update as

ut+1≈A​ut,A:=I+ητ​M.u_{t+1}\approx Au_{t},\qquad A:=I+\frac{\eta}{\tau}M.

If u0u_{0} has a nonzero component along w+w_{+}, then that component is multiplied (at the linearized level) by 1+η​λ+/τ1+\eta\lambda_{+}/\tau at each step. Thus if η​λ+/τ>0\eta\lambda_{+}/\tau>0 (equivalently 1+η​λ+/τ>11+\eta\lambda_{+}/\tau>1), that component grows exponentially, giving linear instability. The temperature dependence is explicit in the multiplicative factor 1+η​λ+/τ1+\eta\lambda_{+}/\tau. For fixed η,λ+>0\eta,\lambda_{+}>0, the map τ↦1+η​λ+/τ\tau\mapsto 1+\eta\lambda_{+}/\tau is strictly decreasing in τ\tau, hence smaller τ\tau produces a larger amplification per step. ∎

Proposition 6.3 formalizes the intuitive picture: once the experts have developed a non-trivial contrast d∗d_{*} with a component along the teacher separator vv, the symmetric router u=0u=0 becomes linearly unstable in an eigendirection that is necessarily correlated with vv. The exact per-step amplification factor is 1+η​λ+/τ1+\eta\lambda_{+}/\tau in the linearized iteration, so smaller router temperature strengthens the local instability for fixed step size.

6.5 Alignment rate and temperature dependence

The same linearization also gives the alignment time scale, but this is only a direct spectral consequence of the update in Proposition 6.3. Let λ1>λ2≥⋯≥λd\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{d} be the eigenvalues of MM, with orthonormal eigenbasis {wi}i=1d\{w_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}, and suppose λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0. If u0=∑iαi(0)​wiu_{0}=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}^{(0)}w_{i} with α1(0)≠0\alpha_{1}^{(0)}\neq 0, then the linearized update ut+1=(I+η​M/τ)​utu_{t+1}=(I+\eta M/\tau)u_{t} gives

αi(t)=(1+ητ​λi)t​αi(0).\alpha_{i}^{(t)}=\Bigl(1+\frac{\eta}{\tau}\lambda_{i}\Bigr)^{t}\alpha_{i}^{(0)}. (6.8)

Under the mild sign-stability condition 1+η​λd/τ>01+\eta\lambda_{d}/\tau>0, the non-leading components decay relative to the leading one according to

αi(t)α1(t)=(1+η​λi/τ1+η​λ1/τ)t​αi(0)α1(0)⟶0,i≥2.\frac{\alpha_{i}^{(t)}}{\alpha_{1}^{(t)}}=\Biggl(\frac{1+\eta\lambda_{i}/\tau}{1+\eta\lambda_{1}/\tau}\Biggr)^{t}\frac{\alpha_{i}^{(0)}}{\alpha_{1}^{(0)}}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad i\geq 2. (6.9)

Thus the normalized direction ut/‖ut‖u_{t}/\|u_{t}\| converges to the leading eigendirection up to sign. Writing

ρ⁡(τ):=1+η​λ2/τ1+η​λ1/τ,\rho(\tau):=\frac{1+\eta\lambda_{2}/\tau}{1+\eta\lambda_{1}/\tau}, (6.10)

the non-leading-to-leading ratio decays geometrically like ρ​(τ)t\rho(\tau)^{t}. In the small-step regime η/τ≪1\eta/\tau\ll 1,

ρ⁡(τ)=1−ητ​(λ1−λ2)+O⁡((η/τ)2),talign≍τη⁡(λ1−λ2).\rho(\tau)=1-\frac{\eta}{\tau}(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2})+O\!\left((\eta/\tau)^{2}\right),\qquad t_{\mathrm{align}}\asymp\frac{\tau}{\eta(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2})}. (6.11)

For fixed η\eta and τ↓0\tau\downarrow 0 with λ1,λ2>0\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>0, however, ρ⁡(τ)→λ2/λ1\rho(\tau)\to\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1}, so the alignment rate saturates rather than continuing to scale like 1/τ1/\tau.

This calculation keeps the symmetry-breaking result at the right scale. It is a short-time, near-symmetric statement for a reduced linearized update in which the expert contrast is treated as slowly varying input to the router. In that regime, smaller τ\tau increases the multiplicative factor 1+η​λ+/τ1+\eta\lambda_{+}/\tau and accelerates the onset of specialization. It does not prove global convergence of the full coupled MoE training dynamics. Rather, it complements the conditional landscape-transfer theorem from the previous section by exhibiting one concrete local mechanism through which a symmetric router can be pushed toward a teacher-aligned partition.

7 What the Results Do and Do Not Show

The results in this paper should be read in a precise way. The unconditional contribution is the boundary-layer analysis of the soft-to-hard routing limit. For a fixed router and expert class, the difference between the soft objective LτL_{\tau} and the hard objective L0L_{0} is controlled by the amount of input probability near the routing interfaces. More concretely, when the top-two logit gap

Δ⁡(x,ϕ)\Delta(x;\phi)

has a polynomial margin tail near zero, the excess contribution of the soft router is localized to the set where Δ⁡(x,ϕ)\Delta(x;\phi) is of order τ\tau. This is the mechanism behind the quantitative soft-to-hard bounds and the Γ\Gamma-convergence statement.

This part of the paper does not require a teacher–student model, realizability, or a global benign-landscape assumption. It is a geometric statement about low-temperature routing. The key object is not the full softmax map, but the probability mass of thin neighborhoods of the hard-routing boundaries.

The landscape result has a different status. It is a transfer theorem. It says that if the profiled hard-routing objective has a stable local minimizer, and if the soft objective approximates the hard objective sufficiently well at the level of the objective, gradient, and Hessian, then the corresponding soft objective has a nearby local minimizer for small temperature. Thus the theorem does not prove that mixture-of-experts training landscapes are generally benign. It proves that favorable local geometry, once present in the hard problem, is stable under the soft-to-hard approximation.

The Gaussian example should also be interpreted narrowly. It is not intended as a model of full-scale MoE training. Its role is to show, in a tractable population setting, how routing symmetry can break and how a hard-routing structure can emerge from a smooth objective. The example supports the geometric picture developed in the main theory, but it is not needed for the boundary-mass or Γ\Gamma-convergence results.

The main remaining problem is therefore not the zero-temperature limit itself, but the structure of the limiting hard-routing problem. The present paper reduces part of the MoE analysis to this question. Once the hard-routing partition is fixed or well controlled, the boundary-mass estimates describe how the soft model approaches it. What remains open is to characterize when the profiled hard-routing objective has good local or global geometry in realistic router–expert families.
